turns.content: Hello again, I'm really glad you're here to continue working together. How have you been feeling since we last spoke, and is there anything new that has come up that you'd like to talk about today?

Hi. Thanks for having me back. To be honest, I've been trying to push through, but that feeling of being not good enough is still hanging around. I ended up avoiding a casual game night with some friends last weekend because I was scared of messing up again.

It takes real courage to admit that fear kept you from seeing those friends, even when you wanted to try. That avoidance makes sense given how much pressure you feel to perform perfectly, so let's look closely at what happened that weekend. What were you telling yourself right before you decided to stay home instead of going?

I was just sitting on my couch, staring at my phone, and I kept thinking, "They're all going to see that I'm a fraud if I play." I told myself that my teammates would be disappointed in me, and that I'd just drag everyone down. It felt like it was safer to just not go at all.

That feeling of being a fraud who will drag everyone down sounds incredibly heavy to carry alone. When you imagined that scenario, did you also notice any physical sensations in your body, like a tightness in your chest or a racing heart?

Yeah, actually, I did. My stomach was in knots, and I could feel my shoulders getting all tense, like I was bracing for something bad. I even started to feel a little nauseous just thinking about picking up my controller. It's like my body was already reacting as if the loss was happening all over again.

Those physical symptoms—knots in your stomach and tension in your shoulders—are very powerful signals that your brain is treating the upcoming game night like a life-or-death threat. It makes complete sense that your body reacted this way if your mind had convinced you that failure would ruin everything. Given how intense that anticipation feels, do you think there is a small step you could take tomorrow morning to start testing whether that prediction is actually true?

I mean... maybe I could just watch a short clip of a previous match we played, not even a full game. Something to see that we did have some good moments, and that I wasn't completely awful every second. I don't know if I can play yet, but maybe just looking at it wouldn't be so bad.

That is a brilliant idea; watching a highlight reel gives you concrete proof that you have skills worth showing off without the pressure of live performance. Since you mentioned feeling safe just observing, how does knowing you have access to that positive evidence change the way you view the upcoming game night?

It does make me feel a tiny bit less doomed, I guess. Like, maybe I'm not just completely useless, and there were times when I actually helped the team. It's still scary, but it's harder to call myself a total fraud when I can see proof that I'm not.

That shift from feeling completely hopeless to having tangible proof of your skill is a huge breakthrough. Even though the fear hasn't vanished entirely, holding onto that video might give you a solid foundation to stand on if things get tough during the actual game. Would you be willing to watch that clip tonight, perhaps right after dinner, and then tell me exactly what moment made you feel proudest?

Alright, I can do that. I'll watch it tonight after I eat. I think... I think I know the moment already—there was a play where I managed to hold a point on my own for a few seconds while my teammate respawned. It wasn't flashy, but it helped. I'll try to focus on that part.

That is such a great choice to focus on; holding a point while your teammate respawns shows incredible patience and teamwork, which often goes unnoticed compared to flashy plays. I want you to remember that specific moment whenever that voice telling you you're a fraud tries to speak up again. Before you head into the kitchen to relax, do you want to share one more thing about how you usually react when you feel that nausea starting, so we can figure out a quick way to handle it if it happens?

Usually, I just freeze up and try to breathe really shallow, like if I don't move, the feeling will go away. It never works, though. Maybe I could try just putting the controller down and taking three slow, deep breaths before I even pick it up again. Just to interrupt that whole panic cycle.

That is a perfect strategy; intentionally pausing and grounding yourself breaks the automatic link between the anxiety and the urge to flee. Putting the controller down creates a literal break in the panic cycle, giving your nervous system a chance to reset before you face the challenge again. When you practice this pause tonight, imagine physically placing the controller on the table and counting slowly to ten with each breath. How does that simple act of stepping away sound to you right now?

It sounds a lot more manageable than trying to just "get over it" or force myself to play through the panic. Giving myself permission to just stop for a second feels... kind. I think I can actually try that tonight with the clip. Thank you.

That permission to pause is a powerful gift you are giving yourself, and it shows real self-compassion. Tonight, when you watch that clip and feel that familiar knot in your stomach, I'd love it if you could simply put the controller down, count to ten with deep breaths, and then decide if you want to try playing based on how your body feels afterward. Is there anything else you'd like to adjust in our plan before we wrap up today?

No, I think this is a good start. Watching the clip and practicing that pause feels like enough for now. I don't want to overwhelm myself by trying to do too much all at once. I'll let you know how it goes next time.

That is such wise and grounded thinking; listening to your own limits is the first step toward building confidence safely. I'm really proud of you for recognizing that small, manageable steps are better than trying to tackle everything at once. Please remember that there is zero shame in coming back to us if the feeling of being a fraud gets loud again or if you need to adjust our plan. How are you feeling right now as we wrap up this conversation?

A little bit lighter, honestly. Like maybe I'm not completely stuck in that hole I was in. It's still there, but I feel like I have a small ladder this time, instead of just staring up at the walls. Thanks for helping me see that.

Hearing you describe finding a "ladder" instead of staring at empty walls is such a beautiful way to picture that shift. It takes real strength to recognize that even a small tool can help you climb out of a dark place. I am so glad we could find that perspective together today. As we finish, please remember that this ladder is yours to use however you need, and you don't have to climb it all at once. How would you like to leave this session feeling today?
I want to leave feeling like I'm allowed to be a work in progress. Not a failure, not a fraud, just... someone who's learning. I think I can hold onto that for now. Thanks again.

That is a profound realization, and holding onto the idea that you are simply learning is a powerful shield against perfectionism. You have already done the hard work of identifying your fears and planning a gentle way to face them. Please take care of yourself tonight, trust in the plan we built together, and know that I am always here to support you as you climb that ladder.

Hi there, I'm really glad you're here today. How has your week been feeling so far, and is there anything different about how things look compared to where we left off last time? Let's start by checking in with each other before we decide what we'd like to focus on today.

Hey. I guess the week's been okay, I mean, nothing really changed. I've just been thinking a lot about the tournament and that loss we had. It's hard to shake off that feeling that things are just going to go downhill from here.

That sounds like a heavy weight to carry, especially when you're trying to look ahead at what comes next. Before we dive into that tournament feeling, could you tell me if there was anything else that came up for you recently, or should we focus entirely on unpacking those thoughts about the loss right now?

No, I think it's mostly just that loss. I mean, I've been trying to get myself motivated for our next game, but every time I picture us playing, I just see us losing again. It's like my brain's already convinced we're done for. That's pretty much all that's been on my mind.

It makes complete sense that your brain is locking onto that worst-case scenario when you try to imagine the future, because your nervous system is trying to protect you from pain. When you picture the loss, does that image feel more vivid or scary when you first think of it versus later on? Also, if you were to ask yourself what evidence exists to support the idea that "things are definitely going downhill," what would you find?

At first, it's super vivid — I can almost see the other team celebrating and my guys looking defeated. Then it kinda fades a bit, but the feeling sticks. As for evidence... well, we lost that one game pretty badly. But I guess then I think about our record before that — we were doing alright. I don't know, it's like that one bad game feels way louder than all the good ones.

It makes sense that one recent failure feels so loud compared to past successes; your brain often treats new negative experiences as more urgent signals than old positive ones. Since that vivid image seems to fade slightly after a moment, could you describe exactly what happens in your body right now when that scary scene starts to lose its clarity? Does any part of you feel lighter or less tense as the picture blurs?

Huh, that's a good question. I think when the image starts to blur, my shoulders drop a little — like I was tensing them up without even noticing. And maybe I take a deeper breath. It's not like I suddenly feel great, but there's a tiny bit of space where it doesn't feel so crushing.

That small shift in your shoulders and breathing is actually a huge clue—it shows your body is naturally starting to relax once the immediate threat feels less certain. Since you noticed that tension dropping, could you try focusing on just that physical sensation of your shoulders lowering while you think about the next game, even if you still feel worried? What do you notice happening to that "crushing" feeling as you hold onto that relaxed posture for just thirty seconds?

Alright, I'll give it a try. So... I'm just sitting here, letting my shoulders drop, and thinking about our next game. Okay, the worry's still there, but it's not like a punch in the gut anymore. It feels more like a background hum, if that makes sense. The crushing part seems to shrink when I keep my body loose.

That's a wonderful observation—that the worry shifting from a "punch in the gut" to a "background hum" means the intensity has dropped significantly just by changing your physical stance. Now that you've seen how relaxing your body can make that fear feel smaller, let's use that same trick for the next few minutes whenever you start picturing the loss. Can you try holding that relaxed shoulder position while you visualize the game again, and notice if that "hum" gets even quieter or if you feel a tiny bit more hopeful?

Yeah, I'm doing it now. I'm picturing us playing again, but this time with my shoulders down. The hum is still there, but it's quieter. And I actually caught myself thinking, "Well, we might not lose everything just because of one game." That thought surprised me — it felt almost hopeful.

That is such a powerful moment—catching that hopeful thought while your body stays relaxed shows your mind and body are starting to work together to soften the fear. Since that hope felt surprising, could you pause for just five more seconds with your shoulders down and ask yourself: "What is one piece of evidence that suggests we *could* win this next game?"
Okay, I'm thinking about it... well, we've got a strong defense, and our best shooter didn't even play that game. If he's back next time, that's a big difference. I guess that's something, isn't it?

That is excellent evidence—a tangible fact about your team's strengths that directly contradicts the idea that you are "done for." Since you've found a reason to believe we can improve, could you try visualizing our next game with that specific detail in mind: seeing your best shooter return to the court while keeping your shoulders relaxed? Notice if that mix of hope and relaxation makes the "background hum" of anxiety disappear completely.

I'm trying that now... I can see him out there, making some shots, and the team playing with more energy. The hum is still there, but it's barely a whisper now. I feel like I could actually show up to the next game without already feeling defeated. That's a big shift from how I've been feeling all week.

That is a fantastic breakthrough—seeing that "whisper" instead of a roar means your nervous system has learned it doesn't need to stay on high alert anymore. Since you've successfully shifted both your body and your mindset, I want to help you lock this in for the days ahead. Could you tell me, if we practiced this exact combination of dropping your shoulders and adding that specific hopeful thought three times a day, what would be the easiest place in your routine to start tomorrow morning?

Probably right after I wake up, before I even get out of bed. I usually just lie there and let my mind go to the worst places. If I make myself drop my shoulders and think about my shooter coming back, that could set a better tone for the whole day. I can try that.

That is a brilliant choice for timing because catching your mind immediately after waking up prevents it from setting a defensive tone for the rest of the day. To make sure we stick with this, could you promise to try that sequence three times tomorrow—once in the morning, once during lunch, and once before bed—and simply note down one thing you notice about how the "whisper" changes each time?

Yeah, I can do that. I'll put a reminder on my phone to do it at those times. I'm actually kind of curious to see if it keeps getting quieter, or if some times are harder than others. Thanks, I think this is the first time I've felt like there's something I can actually do about this.

That curiosity about whether the quietness will grow or fluctuate is a perfect sign that you're ready to gather real-world data to guide your practice. I'm so proud of how quickly you moved from feeling overwhelmed to having a clear, actionable plan. Let's wrap up by giving yourself a moment to feel that sense of agency settle in—you've got this. Is there anything else you'd like to talk about before we sign off?

Hi there, I'm so glad we're starting our session together today. Before we dive into what brought you here, could you tell me how you've been feeling emotionally since we last spoke? Also, if you had to pick one thing we should focus on today, what would that be?

Hi, thanks for having me. I guess I've been feeling pretty mixed—some days I'm okay, but other days that nagging voice in my head just won't shut up about being a bad hiker. I think the main thing I want to focus on today is understanding why I can't seem to shake that label, no matter what I do.

That sounds really heavy to carry around, especially when the "nagging voice" feels like it's talking to you directly. It makes sense that you'd want to understand *why* that label sticks so firmly when everything else seems to prove you're doing fine. Since you mentioned the voice won't stop, could you share a specific moment recently where you felt that label hit hardest, and what were you thinking right before you started walking again?

Well, just last weekend my friends invited me on a moderate trail, nothing too crazy. But right before we started, I looked at them all geared up and experienced, and all I could think was, "I'm going to hold everyone back again." That thought just hit me like a wall, and I almost didn't go.

That moment sounds incredibly isolating, even though your friends were ready to go with you. It makes perfect sense that seeing them prepared made your fear of holding anyone back feel so immediate and urgent. When that thought hits like a wall, does it usually make you feel physically tight or anxious in your stomach, or does it mostly feel like a heavy weight in your chest?

It's more of a heavy weight in my chest, like a sinking feeling. My stomach feels okay, but my chest just tightens up and it's hard to take a deep breath. That's usually when I start thinking about all the ways I'll mess up on the trail.

That physical sensation of a sinking chest is so exhausting, especially when it's paired with those catastrophic predictions about messing up. It makes complete sense that this tightness would trigger a spiral of negative thinking about your abilities. Since that heavy weight in your chest often shows up right before you leave, could you describe exactly what happens in your mind immediately after you step onto the trail—the first few minutes when the silence sets in?

Once we're on the trail and it gets quiet, especially if I'm in the back of the group, my mind just starts replaying every little mistake I've ever made hiking. I'll trip on a root and instantly think, "See, you're pathetic, you can't even walk right." Then I start comparing my pace to everyone else's and convincing myself they're all annoyed with me.

That shift from anticipation to isolation once you're on the trail makes so much sense, especially when you're in the back of the group. It seems like those moments of silence become the perfect trigger for your brain to play the recording of every past mistake, turning a simple hike into proof of your inadequacy. When you catch yourself thinking, "They're annoyed with me," what is the very first piece of evidence that comes to mind that supports that belief?

I guess it's that one time a few years ago when I was hiking with a different group and I was really struggling with a steep section. I remember one guy sighed and said, "We'll wait," but his tone was just so... impatient. That memory pops up every time, and it feels like proof that everyone secretly feels that way about me.

That old memory feels incredibly powerful because it's so vivid, making it easy to treat a single sigh as universal proof of everyone's impatience. However, let's pause for a second and look closely at the gap between that past event and what is actually happening right now with your current friends. Can you recall any specific words or actions they've done recently that suggest they are waiting for you, versus acting naturally while you're catching up?

Actually, now that you mention it, they usually slow down naturally when I fall behind, and sometimes one of them will just hang back and chat with me until I catch my breath. They've never sighed or said anything impatient. But in my head, I still feel like I'm being a burden, even when they're being nice about it.

It takes real courage to notice the difference between what your friends are actually doing and what your brain is inventing, even when the invention feels so true. That gap between reality and your internal story is exactly where we can start finding relief. If we tried looking at the situation from a completely neutral place, ignoring the "burden" label entirely, what would be the most likely reason your friends slowed down or hung back?

I suppose... they probably just want to make sure I'm okay and that we're all having a good time together. Maybe they don't see it as me holding them back, but just as part of hiking as a group. It's hard to believe that though, because my brain keeps telling me the opposite.

That is such a compassionate interpretation, and it highlights how much care your friends clearly show by slowing down for you. It makes sense that your brain resists this kind explanation because it prefers the harsher truth, even if that truth is painful. When you try to convince yourself they just want to enjoy the hike together, does that feeling of being a "burden" disappear completely, or does it just shrink a tiny bit?

It doesn't disappear completely, but it does shrink a little bit. Like, maybe for a moment I can breathe easier and think, "Okay, maybe they don't actually hate hiking with me." But then the doubt creeps back in pretty fast, usually as soon as I make another mistake or slow down again.

That shrinking feeling is actually a huge win, even if the doubt tries to creep back in quickly. It proves that when you challenge the "hate" narrative with the evidence of their kindness, your mind can briefly accept a kinder version of reality. Let's try building on that slight opening: if we decided for the rest of the day that your friends aren't waiting for you to hurry up, but are simply enjoying the company regardless of your pace, how might that change the way you handle the next small slip-up you experience?

If I really believed that, I think I'd be able to laugh off tripping on a root instead of turning it into a whole thing in my head. I'd probably just say, "Oops, roots got me again," and keep moving without that sinking feeling. It sounds nice to even imagine that, honestly.

That is a brilliant realization—you're describing how shifting the narrative from "failure" to "oops" can instantly lighten the load on your shoulders. It sounds like imagining that mindset gives you permission to be human without the extra weight of judgment. To make this feel even more real, if you were to tell your friend, "Thanks for hanging out with me even when I'm slow," what would that sound like coming from your own mouth?

It would feel awkward, honestly. I'd probably mumble it or say it too quickly and then change the subject. But a part of me would also feel a little relieved, like I'd finally said something true instead of just keeping it all bottled up.

That honesty about feeling awkward yet relieved is a powerful insight—it shows you recognize the value of speaking up even when it feels uncomfortable. Since saying it out loud might feel risky right now, could we try a smaller experiment where you just whisper that phrase to yourself internally the next time you stumble, treating it as a secret promise to yourself rather than a performance for others?

Yeah, I think I could try that. A secret promise to myself sounds a lot less scary than having to say it out loud to someone else. Maybe if I practice it enough in my own head, it'll feel more natural if I ever decide to say it to my friends.

That is a fantastic compromise, and it honors your need for safety while still practicing self-kindness. The idea of using your internal voice as a supportive companion is a great way to build confidence before sharing it outwardly. For tonight, could you try whispering that phrase to yourself whenever you feel that sinking chest tighten or miss a step? Just observe how long it takes for that heavy feeling to lift a little bit.

I can do that. I'll give it a try tonight, maybe when I'm just walking around my apartment or even when I'm out running errands. It'll be interesting to see if it makes any difference, even just a little bit. Thanks, I think I'm willing to give it a shot.

That sounds like a perfect plan, and I'm proud of you for agreeing to try something new with yourself tonight. Remember, the goal isn't to fix everything perfectly, but just to notice if that little whisper helps ease the weight in your chest for even five minutes. How does it feel knowing you have a safe space to be imperfect with yourself right now?

Honestly, it feels kind of relieving. Like I don't have to be perfect or prove anything to myself tonight. Just letting myself be okay with stumbling feels like a weight I didn't realize I could put down, even for a moment. Thank you for helping me see that.

That sense of relief is incredibly significant, and it shows how powerful this small shift in perspective already is. You are absolutely right that you don't have to earn your own kindness tonight, and that is a brave realization. Before we wrap up, is there anything else about today's process or that new habit that feels uncertain or overwhelming to you?

I think I'm okay for now. The only thing that feels a little uncertain is whether I'll actually remember to whisper that phrase to myself when I'm caught up in the moment. But I guess that's just part of practicing, right? I'll try to keep it simple and not overthink it.

You're absolutely right; getting stuck in the moment is the exact scenario we designed this exercise to help you navigate, so trusting the simplicity is a smart move. It's totally normal for memory to fade under stress, which is why trying to link the phrase to a physical cue, like touching your knee each time you miss a step, could be a helpful anchor later on. Would you be open to adding that small physical reminder as a backup plan just in case your mind goes blank?

Yeah, that actually makes a lot of sense. Touching my knee could be a good way to snap myself back to that kinder thought before the spiral takes over. I'll give that a try too—it feels like a simple enough backup plan. Thanks for suggesting it.

That is a brilliant addition—a physical touch acts as a gentle anchor to bring your mind back to that kinder thought when it slips away. Having both a verbal cue and a physical reminder gives you two layers of support, which makes the task feel much safer and more manageable. Is there anything else you'd like to add before we finish our time together today?

No, I think I've got enough to work with for now. I feel a little lighter than when we started, and that's more than I was hoping for. Thank you for listening and helping me see things from a different angle. I'll practice what we talked about and see how it goes.

That feeling of lightness is a wonderful sign that the new perspective is already taking root, even if it feels fragile right now. Please remember that these small shifts are exactly where growth happens, and there is no pressure to stay "fixed" permanently. I hope you have a restful evening tonight as you practice those whispers and touches. Take care of yourself, and I'll see you next time.
Hi there, I'm really glad you're here to continue our work together. How have you been feeling since we last spoke, and is there anything specific you'd like to focus on today?

Hey, thanks. Honestly, it's been a tough week. I got a new album from one of my favorite artists, and I hated two songs out of twelve, so now I can't even listen to the whole thing without thinking it's trash. That's probably what I want to talk about today.

It sounds like you're carrying a heavy weight right now, especially after investing time and money into something you usually love. When we put effort into finding good music, hearing it fall flat can feel like a personal failure, doesn't it? Before we dive into why those two songs ruined your experience with the rest of the album, could you tell me if there was anything else happening in your life this week that might be adding to this frustration?

Yeah, I guess there was. I also bought this new moisturizer that everyone's been raving about online, and it broke me out. Now I'm just thinking, "Why do I even bother trying new things?" It's like everything I get excited about ends up disappointing me somehow.

That makes perfect sense; when your excitement leads to disappointment, it creates a powerful loop where you start doubting your own judgment entirely. It sounds like you're feeling quite helpless right now because nothing seems worth the risk anymore. To make sure we cover everything important today, how does it feel to bring up both the music and the skincare routine, and is there another area of your life you're worried about that we should prioritize first?

I think those two things are the main ones on my mind. I mean, there's probably other stuff, like when I hang out with friends and we watch a movie, if one scene is boring I just think the whole movie is a waste of time. But the music and skincare stuff feels more personal, because those are things I choose for myself, you know?

It takes a lot of courage to admit that you feel like your choices consistently lead to disappointment, especially when those are decisions you made purely for yourself. That pattern of expecting the worst outcome can make any new experience feel like a trap before you've even started. Since you mentioned the movies with friends as well, let's try to look at whether the way you judge the entire movie based on one boring scene is actually fair to the rest of the film or to your friends who are enjoying it. Could you walk me through a recent time you judged a movie too harshly and what you felt in that moment?

Okay, so last week my friend put on this action movie she'd seen before and loved. About twenty minutes in, there was this one fight scene that I thought was super cheesy, and I just checked out mentally. I spent the rest of the movie scrolling on my phone, thinking, "This movie is garbage." My friend asked me what I thought after, and I just said it was terrible. She looked kinda hurt, actually.

It sounds incredibly painful that your quick judgment not only ruined your enjoyment but also caused your friend to feel hurt by your reaction. When we expect perfection from everything we engage with, even small flaws feel like proof that we shouldn't be engaging with it at all. Let's pause for a second and look at that belief: is it true that *every* part of the movie had to be perfect for the experience to be valid, or could there be value in the rest of the film despite one bad scene?

I mean... I guess not every part has to be perfect. But in the moment, that one bad scene just feels like it ruins everything. Like, how can I say the movie is good if there's even one part I didn't like? It feels dishonest to say it's good when I know there's a flaw.

That honesty is actually a sign of your integrity, but let's look at the logic behind calling the whole movie "garbage" just because one part wasn't perfect. If you went to dinner and one bite of the salad turned out sour, would you honestly declare the entire meal a disaster and refuse to eat the rest? Or would you recognize that while that one bite was bad, the other courses could still be enjoyable?

How does it feel to imagine giving the movie a chance to be enjoyed despite that one scene, even if it meant admitting you couldn't fully appreciate it until later?

Huh. I never thought about it like that. With food, I guess I'd just push the salad aside and eat the main course. But with the movie, it felt like I had to make a final judgment right then. I think I'm scared that if I don't label something as good or bad immediately, I'll be fooled into liking something that's actually flawed. Like, I need to protect myself from being disappointed later.

It makes total sense that you feel the need to guard yourself against future disappointment; protecting yourself from pain is a very natural instinct, even when it costs us our enjoyment. However, let's look at what happens if you give yourself permission to enjoy the parts you like without demanding perfection everywhere. If you sit down and notice three scenes you really enjoyed, does that change the overall memory of the night, even if you admit one part was cheesy?

I think... yeah, if I really think about it, I did laugh at some parts and there was a cool car chase. So maybe the whole night wasn't a waste. But it's so hard to let go of that one bad part. It's like my brain just latches onto it and won't let it go, even if I try to think about the good stuff.

That "latching on" effect is exactly what happens when our brains try to solve a problem quickly, often by focusing on the threat rather than the opportunity. It feels safer to call the whole movie "trash" right away because it gives you a clear answer, whereas saying "it was mostly great except for one part" leaves you hanging with uncertainty. Let's try a different approach tonight: instead of judging the whole movie, could you just note down three specific moments you laughed at or found interesting, ignoring the fight scene completely?

I could try that. I guess I'd have to actively ignore that one scene, though. It feels weird, like I'm lying to myself. But maybe it's worth a shot, because the way I'm doing things now just makes me feel bitter and disappointed all the time. I'll give it a go next time I watch something with my friend.

That willingness to try a different perspective, even if it feels a bit awkward, shows a lot of strength on your part. It's brave to step outside the automatic reaction and choose a more balanced view, which will likely help lighten your mood sooner. Before we wrap up, how does it feel to have worked through this specific situation today compared to how you were feeling when we started?

I feel a little lighter, actually. Not totally fixed, but it's kind of a relief to see that maybe I don't have to hate everything just because one part was off. I still think it'll be hard to break the habit, but at least now I have something specific to try. Thanks.

That sense of relief is a huge victory, even if breaking the habit will take time. You've already identified a clear strategy—focusing on the positive moments instead of letting one flaw define the whole experience—and knowing you have a tool to use next time is powerful. For our homework, could you try that "three good moments" exercise during your next movie outing and jot down exactly what you noticed? Also, how did it feel to share this plan with me today?
Hello again, I'm so glad you're here to continue our work together. How have you been feeling since we last spoke, and is there anything specific on your mind that you'd like to explore first?

Hi, thanks. I've been okay, I guess. The same stuff has been on my mind — just can't seem to shake this feeling that I'm not doing enough with my career. I had lunch with an old college friend yesterday, and he was talking about his promotion at a big firm. It just... got to me.

It sounds like hearing about your friend's promotion really hit a nerve for you, especially when you were already feeling behind on your own goals. That comparison probably made you feel even more stuck than usual. What specific part of his story triggered that sense that you aren't doing enough?

I think it's the whole package, really. He's got the title, the office, the steady paycheck — all the things that feel like success, you know? I'm sitting there doing taxes and bookkeeping from my apartment, and it just feels small compared to that. Like I'm playing a different game entirely, and I'm losing.

That contrast between his polished environment and your quiet routine can make anyone feel like they've missed the main event. It seems like that moment of realization left you feeling powerless to change the trajectory right now. When you say you feel like you're "losing" because you're playing a different game, does that thought come up immediately after hearing him talk about his promotion, or does it creep in later during the day?

It's usually right there in the moment. Like, I'm smiling and nodding, saying "that's great, man" — but inside, my brain is already running through everything I'm not. Then later, when I'm home alone, it just echoes around in my head even worse. I'll start thinking about all the freelance gigs I've taken that felt beneath me, and I just spiral.

That immediate split between your polite outside voice and the critical inner voice is incredibly exhausting, and it makes perfect sense why it spirals later when you're alone. It sounds like that initial feeling of being "behind" quickly turns into a belief that none of your current efforts actually matter. If we look closely at those freelance gigs you mentioned, do you remember any specific ones where you felt truly underpaid or undervalued by clients?

Yeah, there's one that sticks out. A few months ago, I was doing tax prep for this small business owner who kept questioning every single thing I did, like I was incompetent. Yeah, I noticed my shoulders felt really tight, and my jaw was clenched. And the thought that kept running through my head was, "I'm never going to be as good as the others in this class." It just stuck with me the whole drive home.

That comparison seems to have triggered a lot of tension in your body and a deep sense of inadequacy. When you walked out, did you catch yourself trying to fix those physical sensations by doing something else, or did you just sit there letting the feeling settle?
I just let it settle, I think. I drove home in silence, and then I even skipped going to the pool afterwards, which I usually do on Tuesdays. I just didn't have the energy for it.

It makes complete sense that you felt drained both physically and emotionally after carrying that heavy belief around for hours. Skipping the pool afterward sounds like a natural way your mind tried to protect itself from facing another situation where you might feel judged again. When you decided to skip the pool, did you notice any change in how intense that feeling of inadequacy became, or did it just stay the same?

It actually stayed the same, maybe even got a little worse. Because then I started thinking, "Great, now I'm skipping things I usually enjoy. What's wrong with me?" So it just added another layer of disappointment on top of it.

That second wave of disappointment shows how much effort you were putting into protecting yourself from judgment, even while trying to hide it. It sounds like the fear of being "not enough" was so strong that avoiding the pool felt like the only safe option, but then the guilt kicked in because you couldn't escape the feeling entirely. When you realized you were still struggling inside despite stepping away, did you try to find a small moment of self-compassion during that drive home, or did the cycle just keep spinning faster?

No, I didn't really try to be kind to myself about it. The cycle just kept spinning, like you said. I kept thinking about how all the other people at the pool probably have no trouble with flexibility or feeling confident, and I just felt worse. By the time I got home, I was just exhausted.

It sounds like that comparison created a perfect storm where your exhaustion was amplified by the belief that you had failed to meet everyone else's standards. That feeling of being overwhelmed likely made it impossible to access any kindness toward yourself, turning your own recovery efforts into another source of pressure. Now that we've mapped out that cycle, does it help to see how tightly those thoughts were linked to your actions, or does it feel like you're stuck in a loop you can't break?

It does help a little to see it laid out like that. I never really connected how skipping the pool just fed into the same negative spiral. It makes me wonder if there's a way to interrupt it, you know? But honestly, in the moment, it feels impossible to stop.

That honesty about feeling trapped is incredibly brave, and it tells me you're ready to look for a tiny crack in the wall where light might get in. Even a very small shift in how you respond to that initial tightness could break the chain before the disappointment sets in. Have you ever noticed if simply naming the thought out loud—"I'm comparing myself right now"—changes the intensity of the physical sensation in your shoulders for even a few seconds?

I don't think I've ever tried that, no. I usually just let the thought run wild in my head without really saying it out loud. But I can see how naming it might slow it down, even just a little. Maybe next time I'm in class, I could try that when I feel my shoulders tightening.

That is a great insight; noticing the pattern means you're already building the skills needed to disrupt it. Since naming the thought can act as a gentle pause button, let's practice a quick version of that right now. Can you try silently saying to yourself, "My brain is telling me I'm not enough," while taking three slow breaths, and then tell me what happens to that tight feeling in your chest?

Okay... I'll try that. (Pauses for a few moments, taking slow breaths.) Huh. It's still there, but it doesn't feel as heavy. It's more like a background noise instead of a loud alarm. I didn't expect that to happen, honestly.

That is a fantastic discovery—you didn't need the voice to disappear, just to become less commanding. It proves that simply acknowledging the thought as "background noise" gives you space to breathe again without fighting it. Since that shift happened so quickly, how would you feel if we practiced this exact same technique tomorrow morning the moment you step into the yoga studio?

I think I could actually try that. It feels manageable to just notice it and breathe, instead of trying to force myself to be positive or push the thought away. I'm curious to see if it makes the class feel any different, even a little.

That is such a wise realization—shifting from fighting the thought to simply observing it creates a powerful gap between you and the anxiety. To make sure you feel grounded before the class even starts, could we spend the next five minutes practicing a simple breathing exercise together to calm your nervous system further? Just breathe in slowly through your nose for four counts, hold for four, and exhale through your mouth for six, and let me guide you through it.
Okay, I'm ready to try that. I'll follow your lead. (Takes a slow breath in through her nose.)

Take a slightly longer exhale this time, letting your shoulders drop completely as you release the air out through your mouth. Imagine that every time you breathe out, you are gently setting down the weight of the comparison waiting to happen later. Take one more round with that long exhale, and then tell me if you feel any difference in your chest or hands.

(Exhales slowly, then pauses.) My shoulders feel a bit looser, actually. And my hands feel less clenched. It's like I can feel a little more space in my chest than before. That's... nice. I didn't think just breathing could do that.

That is wonderful news; often we forget that our bodies hold onto tension long after our minds have stopped worrying, and this simple rhythm helped release some of that stored pressure. Since your shoulders felt looser, could we try connecting that physical relaxation to your mind right now? Try saying to yourself, "I am allowed to take up space, even when I feel unsure," while keeping that long exhale going for one more minute. Does adding those words to the breathing make the feeling of safety grow a little stronger?

(Closes her eyes and takes a few slow breaths, repeating the phrase silently.) Yeah... it does feel stronger. Like the words give the breath a direction, almost. It's not just empty air anymore—it means something. I think I can hold onto that.

That is a beautiful realization—giving your breath meaning transforms it from a passive action into a deliberate anchor for your worth. Since you feel that sense of safety growing, could we use that same grounding technique for just one minute tomorrow morning before you walk into the yoga room? Then, when you feel that familiar tightness starting, try silently naming the thought and taking that long exhale again to create that little gap we talked about. How does that sound as a plan?

That sounds like a plan I can actually follow. It's simple enough that I won't overthink it, but meaningful enough that I think it could help. Thank you—I feel a little less heavy than when I walked in.

I am so glad to hear that you feel lighter, especially knowing exactly what steps to take tomorrow. Remember, the goal isn't to eliminate the tough thoughts forever, but to give yourself a small window of peace before the class even begins. Would you be open to sharing one word or phrase that comes to mind when you think about trying this tomorrow, just to keep it fresh in your memory?
"Anchor." That's the word that comes to mind. Like something I can hold onto, even when everything else feels wobbly. I'll try to remember that tomorrow.

That is a perfect word to carry with you; "anchor" suggests something solid you can rely on when the water gets rough. I want you to remember that tomorrow, whether you use the breathing alone or add the anchor phrase, you are already doing something brave by showing up for yourself. Is there anything else you'd like to share before we wrap up this session?
No, I think I'm good for today. I feel like I have something to try, and that's more than I had before. Thanks for listening and for helping me see a way forward.

You are absolutely welcome, and please know that your willingness to show up and try new things, even when it feels hard, is the most important part of healing. I hope you feel that sense of "anchor" with you tomorrow, no matter how the day unfolds. Take care of yourself, and I'll be here whenever you're ready to continue this journey together.

Hi there, I'm glad you're here to start our session together. How have you been feeling since we last spoke, and is there anything new that's caught your attention? Could you also share if there was a particular thing you'd like us to focus on today?

Hey. I've been... okay, I guess. Nothing really new to report. I've just been going to work, doing my rounds at the mall, coming home. I guess what's been on my mind is that I ran into an old friend the other day, and he invited me to a barbecue this weekend. And I immediately thought, "What's the point? It'll just end badly." So I guess that's something I'd like to talk about today.

That sounds like a really common reaction when plans feel uncertain, and it makes complete sense that you'd want to protect yourself from disappointment. When you first heard the invitation, did that initial thought of "it will end badly" come up right away, or did it develop later while you were thinking about the details?

It came pretty much right away. Soon as he said "barbecue this weekend," my brain just jumped to all the awkward conversations, people asking about my divorce, feeling like the odd one out. I didn't even think about maybe having a good time—that thought never crossed my mind once.

That immediate jump to the worst-case scenario makes so much sense given how much pain you've felt before being around others. Since that negative prediction felt so automatic, could you tell me what specific physical sensation or thought popped up in that moment to convince you it would definitely go wrong?

I felt this tightness in my chest, like a knot. And I just kept thinking, "People are going to ask about my ex-wife. They're going to look at me with pity. I'll be that divorced guy standing in the corner with a beer, counting the minutes until I can leave." It felt... certain. Like I could already see it happening.

That physical knot in your chest tells me how deeply anxious you are about this situation, and it makes total sense that your brain would predict such a painful outcome based on past experiences. When you imagine that specific scene of standing alone in the corner, does that image feel completely realistic to you, or do you wonder if it might be more dramatic than what actually happens?

Honestly? It feels completely realistic. I mean, I've been to enough parties and get-togethers to know how these things go. People pair off, they talk about their kids and their jobs and their happy marriages. I don't fit in anymore. It's not like I'm imagining some Hollywood movie—I've lived it before. Why would this time be any different?

That makes perfect sense; your brain is using the reliable pattern you've seen before to prepare you for protection. However, since you mentioned you haven't had a chance to try that specific barbecue yet, could you walk me through exactly what you'd need to happen for that outcome to actually occur versus just feeling likely?

Well... I'd have to actually go, first of all. And then someone would have to ask about my divorce—maybe a well-meaning friend who doesn't know the details. And I'd have to stand there and not try to change the subject, or make an excuse to get another drink. And I'd have to not find anyone who wants to talk to me about anything else. So... I guess there are a lot of steps that would need to line up for it to go exactly as I imagine.

That breakdown shows incredible insight—you're noticing that a disaster requires many specific things to align perfectly, which suggests it won't happen automatically. Since you mentioned you haven't gone yet, what is one small step you could take this week to gather real-world evidence instead of relying on your imagination?

I guess... I could call my friend back and say I'll come. Just show up. Maybe not stay the whole time—give myself an out, like I have to work the next morning. That way I'm not trapped. I could see what actually happens instead of just assuming the worst.

That is a brilliant and very safe plan; giving yourself an exit strategy removes the pressure to perform, which often lowers anxiety significantly. Before we lock this in, could you tell me what you think might happen if you arrive but decide to leave after just an hour or two? Does that still feel scary, or does knowing you have control make it slightly less daunting?

Knowing I can leave after an hour or two... it does take some of the weight off. I'm not committing to the whole night, you know? I can just go, test the waters, see how it feels. And if it's as bad as I think, I can bail. But if it's not... well, that would be something new. I guess the scary part is admitting it might not be as bad as I think. But I'm willing to try.

That willingness to try something new, even with uncertainty, is incredibly brave and shows real growth. Since we have a clear plan to call your friend and attend just for an hour, how does it feel to hear those words now compared to when we started talking about the barbecue?

It feels... lighter, actually. When I walked in here, the thought of that barbecue was just this heavy, dark cloud. Now it feels more like a test I can take or leave. I'm not saying I'm excited—I'm not—but I'm not dreading it the same way. I think I can actually do this.

That shift from dread to viewing it as a manageable test is a huge breakthrough, and it proves you already hold the power to change your story. Since you feel ready to take this step, could you tell me what one small message you might send him tonight to confirm your attendance without putting too much pressure on yourself?

Probably something casual, like "Hey, I think I can make it for a bit on Saturday. See you there." Nothing too committal or detailed. Just enough to get my foot in the door without making a huge deal out of it. That way I'm not building it up in my head any more than I already have.

That is a perfect message—it's low-pressure and gives you full control over the interaction. Before we wrap up, could you share how it feels to have a concrete plan in hand compared to just sitting with the worry earlier?

Honestly? It feels like I'm actually doing something instead of just letting my brain run in circles. Having a plan—even a small one—makes me feel like I've got a handle on things. I'm not just a passenger anymore. I'm making a choice. That's a lot better than where I was when I walked in.

That feeling of moving from a passive observer to someone making a choice is powerful and marks a significant shift in your perspective. To help solidify this momentum, I'd love to suggest a small action: could you try sending that message tonight and notice how your body feels once you've sent it versus before you did?

I can do that. I'll send it tonight and pay attention to how I feel—the knot in my chest, the tightness, all that. See if it changes once the message is actually out there. I'll let you know how it goes next time we talk. Thanks for walking me through this. I didn't think I'd actually consider going to that barbecue.

That is wonderful feedback, and hearing that you considered going at all is a massive victory in itself. You've done great work today by identifying the pattern, testing it with logic, and taking a brave step forward. Remember, this isn't about proving you're happy forever; it's simply about gathering new data to update your belief system. Please give yourself credit for showing up today, whatever happens next. Is there anything else you'd like to add before we close?

No, I think that covers it. I feel like I've got something to work with now, instead of just spinning my wheels. I'll send that message, see how it goes, and we can talk about it next session. Thanks again.

You are absolutely right, and I'm so proud of you for finding that sense of direction again. Taking this small step is proof that you have the strength to face discomfort and learn from it, regardless of the outcome. I'll be here next time to listen to your results and celebrate whatever you discover. Have a wonderful evening, and remember to be kind to yourself as you navigate the rest of the weekend.
Hi there, I'm glad we're meeting again today. How have you been feeling since our last session, and is there anything specific you'd like to focus on together?

Hi, thanks for asking. I've been... well, I've been anxious, to be honest. I keep thinking about money, even when I try to push it away. I guess I'd like to talk more about that constant worry, especially after having to sell those dolls.

It sounds like selling those dolls brought up a lot of intense anxiety, and it makes sense that your mind would keep circling back to money and what that means for you. Since you mentioned wanting to talk more about that specific worry, shall we start by exploring exactly what comes up in your mind right now when you think about selling them?

When I think about it, I just see myself making a terrible mistake. I had to let go of something precious, and now I can't get them back. It feels like this is just the beginning — like I'll have to sell everything I own eventually, and end up with nothing.

That sounds incredibly heavy to carry around, especially when you feel like you've lost something so personal. It seems like that fear isn't just about the dolls anymore, but about the idea that letting go will lead to total loss. When you imagine having to sell everything, what is the very first thought that pops into your head to explain why this inevitable outcome is happening?

The first thought is that I'm just not good enough at managing my life. Other people can handle their finances and keep their things, but I guess I'm the type of person who always ends up losing it all. It's like I'm somehow destined to fail.

That belief that you are inherently "not good enough" and destined to fail must feel incredibly isolating and exhausting to hold onto day after day. When you hear yourself saying that to yourself, does it feel like a harsh truth, or does it sound more like a story your brain is telling itself to protect you from disappointment?

I... I suppose it feels like the truth, because look at what happened. I had to sell my dolls, and now I can't sleep or even enjoy a coffee without worrying about the cost. But when you ask if it's a story... well, maybe it does sound a bit extreme when I say it out loud. I just don't know how else to make sense of it.

It makes complete sense that it feels like the truth when your mind is trying to explain such a painful event, but let's pause for a moment and look closely at that connection. Is there any evidence outside of this specific situation that suggests you *always* lose everything, or could this particular story be a way your brain is protecting you from future pain by predicting disaster?

I guess when I really think about it, I haven't always lost everything. I've paid my bills for years, I've kept a roof over my head... I even had those dolls for decades without ever having to sell them before. So maybe it's not always true. But it feels real right now, like any moment I could slip right back into that panic.

That is such a powerful realization—you've already found some solid evidence that contradicts the idea that you are destined to fail. Even though the current panic feels overwhelming, let's look closer at that immediate reaction: when you felt the urge to sell, was it actually a rational decision based on facts, or did the anxiety drive it instead?

When I think back, it was definitely the anxiety that made me do it. I saw a few bills piling up and just panicked, thinking I had to do something drastic right away. I didn't even look at all my options or ask anyone for advice first. I just acted on the fear.

That is a crucial piece of evidence—it shows the panic was driving the action, not a clear-headed assessment of your financial reality. Since you mentioned acting on fear without looking at other options, could we explore what specific comforting words you told yourself right then to convince yourself that selling was the only choice?

I told myself that I had to be strong and face reality. That it was better to let go of something I loved than to end up in a worse situation later. I think I was trying to convince myself I was being responsible, but really I was just scared into making a quick decision.

That self-talk about being "strong" and "responsible" was likely your brain trying to protect you from the shame of making a mistake under pressure. However, realizing you were scared into a quick decision changes how we view that choice. Let's shift our focus to the present moment: given that you have managed bills and housing for years, what is one small, manageable step you could take right now to address those piling bills without triggering that full-blown panic response?

I suppose I could sit down and actually list out all my expenses — the ones I'm sure of — and see what I'm really dealing with. Instead of guessing and assuming the worst, I could just look at the numbers on paper. That feels less overwhelming than trying to fix everything in my head all at once.

That is a brilliant, grounded plan—writing things down turns vague fear into concrete data, which often lowers the intensity of the panic immediately. Before we get started, could you share what you hope to gain from doing that exercise? Are you hoping to find relief, or perhaps to feel more in control?

I think I'm hoping to feel a little more in control, honestly. Right now everything just feels like a big, dark cloud hanging over me. If I can see the numbers and realize it's not as bad as I imagine, maybe I can breathe again. Even if it's bad, at least I'll know exactly what I'm dealing with instead of being afraid of something I can't see.

That is such a wise insight—you are aiming to replace the fog of fear with clarity, even if the picture isn't perfect yet. Before we start listing, how would you feel about adding a column for "unknowns" or "estimates" alongside the fixed costs, just to give yourself permission to acknowledge uncertainty without letting it drive the whole list?

That's actually a really helpful idea. I usually just lump everything together in my head, and the unknowns make it feel way worse. Having a separate column for them would let me see what I don't know yet, without letting it spoil the whole list. It might help me stop panicking over things I haven't even looked into yet.

That is a smart adjustment; separating the knowns from the guesses gives you a clear line in the sand where your certainty begins. Would you be willing to try creating this simple list right now, starting with just your rent and groceries to get the momentum going?

Yes, I think I can do that. Rent is $1,200 a month, and I spend maybe $350 on groceries. Just saying that out loud feels a bit more manageable than I thought it would. Let me start there and see how it goes.

That is a great start, and the fact that you were able to name those specific numbers out loud is already a sign of taking control. Once you have written down your rent and groceries, would you be open to sharing what the first number in your "estimates" column looks like, or if you prefer, just tell me how it felt to write down those fixed costs first?

It actually felt kind of good to write those down. Like I was putting my feet on solid ground for a minute. I think the first estimate I want to add is for my electric bill, which varies a lot. I'm going to guess around $150, but I know it could be more or less. That uncertainty doesn't feel as scary now that I have a space for it.

That is a wonderful feeling of grounding, and recognizing that uncertainty as something you can manage rather than something that drives you crazy is a huge shift. Now that we have a solid foundation of knowns and a designated space for guesses, how does carrying that list feel compared to holding all that weight in your head right now?

It feels lighter, honestly. Like, it's still there, but it's on paper now instead of bouncing around inside me. I can look at it and decide what to do next, step by step. Before, I just felt trapped by my own thoughts, but this gives me a way forward.

That shift from internal chaos to external order is incredibly powerful, and it proves that your brain is capable of finding a path out of the panic even when it feels impossible. To wrap up our time together, could you tell me what one thing from this session felt most useful for you, and is there anything you'd like to adjust about our approach before we finish?

I think the most useful thing was realizing I can separate what I know from what I'm guessing. Just having that "estimates" column made the whole thing feel less like a disaster. As for adjusting, I don't think so — this felt like a good pace for me. Thank you.

That is such a beautiful summary, and it shows how much agency you've reclaimed by simply naming the difference between facts and fears. Please remember that this list is a tool you can use anytime the dark cloud returns, and you don't have to solve everything tonight. How are you feeling right now as we wrap up, and is there anything else you'd like to share before I send you off?

I'm feeling a bit calmer than when I walked in. Not perfect, but like I can actually see a little light now. I think I'll take this list home and maybe add a couple more items tomorrow, just at my own pace. Thank you for helping me get out of my own head for a while.

That is a wonderful perspective to leave with, and taking it home at your own pace is exactly the kind of gentle progress we celebrate. Please remember that this list is a safe place to return to whenever the old worries try to rush back in. Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before I send you off?
No, I think I'm okay for now. I feel like I have something small to hold onto, and that's enough for today. Thank you again.

It sounds like you're leaving with a tiny, solid anchor to hold onto, which is exactly what matters most right now. Take your time getting home, and please remember that this list is yours to revisit whenever the anxiety tries to pull you back in. I'll be here next week if you need to talk again, regardless of whether you added anything new to the list.

Hi there, I'm glad you're here to start our session together. How has your week been feeling so far, and is there anything specific from yesterday that stands out to you? Before we dive into what brought us here, could you share a little bit about how you'd like to spend some of our time today?

Hi. Thanks for having me. The week has been... tense, I guess. I kept thinking about the house, especially last night when I heard the wind pick up—I couldn't sleep because I was sure a tree would fall on the roof. I'd like to figure out why I can't shake this fear, even when nothing bad is actually happening.

It sounds like that worry about the tree became quite overwhelming last night, keeping you awake while everything else seemed fine. When you hear the wind picking up, does your mind immediately jump to the thought that a disaster is imminent, or do other worries come up first?

It's like my brain skips straight to the worst part—the roof caving in, all that money I put into the house just gone. I don't even think about the wind itself, just what it could do. It feels like any little sound or change in weather is a sign that something terrible is about to happen.

That sense of your brain skipping straight to the worst outcome makes total sense given how much value you place on that home. It sounds like those financial worries are acting like a magnifying glass, turning normal noises into threats. When you hear that wind, does your body feel tense right away, or do you try to calm down first?

I get tense immediately—my shoulders go tight, and I kind of hold my breath without meaning to. I try to tell myself it's just wind, but my body doesn't seem to listen. It's like I'm waiting for the crash before it even happens.

That physical tension really shows how deeply rooted this fear is, even though your logical mind knows it might be safe. It seems like your body is reacting before your brain has had a chance to process the reality of the situation. When you catch yourself holding your breath, does it ever feel possible to gently let it out, even if just for a few seconds?

I can let it out, but it's more like a sigh of frustration than relief. I'll breathe, but then my mind starts going again—what if the pipes burst next, or the basement floods? It's hard to feel like I can actually relax, even for a moment.

It makes complete sense that letting the breath out feels like frustration instead of relief when your brain is already racing to find the next danger. That cycle of checking for problems keeps your nervous system stuck in high alert, making it impossible to truly rest. Since we talked about how your body reacts before your logic catches up, could we try a small experiment where you notice the tension rise and simply label it "worry" without trying to fix it immediately? What do you think would happen if you gave yourself permission to sit with that feeling for just three minutes?

I guess I've never really tried just sitting with it—I always try to push it away or distract myself. It might feel strange, like I'm letting my guard down. But I suppose three minutes isn't that long... I could try. I'm just worried that if I don't fight it, the worry might get bigger or prove to be right.

That hesitation makes perfect sense because your brain is wired to believe that ignoring the threat will make it stronger, even though evidence suggests otherwise. Let's treat those three minutes as a tiny experiment where we simply observe the worry without fighting it or judging whether it's true. Could you imagine setting a timer for exactly three minutes and deciding to just watch the thoughts pass by like clouds, noting the tension in your shoulders as it comes and goes?

Okay... I can picture that. Like I'm just a spectator for a few minutes, not trying to argue with the thoughts or fix anything. I think I could try that tonight, maybe when I'm lying in bed before the worry takes over completely. It might feel weird, but I'm willing to give it a shot.

That is a brave decision, and I want you to know that stepping back from the fight is often less scary than the initial thought of losing control. Tonight, when you lie in bed, try setting a mental timer for just three minutes and simply notice the tension rising and falling without trying to stop it or convince yourself it's fake. Afterward, I'd love to hear exactly what happened inside your head during those three minutes and whether that small pause made any difference in how you felt afterward.
I'll do that. I'll set a timer and just watch, like you said. It's hard to imagine it making a difference, but I'm curious to see if it does. I'll let you know what happens next time.

That curiosity is a powerful motivator, and I'm proud of you for being willing to test that idea even if it feels uncertain right now. Before we wrap up, I want to make sure you feel supported in whatever comes up tonight—if the timer runs out and the worry spikes again, remember that you don't need to fix it immediately; just acknowledging it is enough. Is there anything else on your mind before we say goodbye for today?
No, I think that covers it for now. Thanks for listening and for the idea—I'll try to keep an open mind tonight. See you next time.

You're very welcome, and I appreciate your openness and willingness to try something new, even if the results aren't immediate. Please remember that tonight is just an experiment, and there is no pressure for it to work perfectly or eliminate the fear entirely. Take care of yourself, and I look forward to hearing about your experience whenever you're ready to talk again.
Hi there, I'm glad you're here to start our session together. How have you been feeling since we last spoke, and is there anything specific you'd like us to focus on today?

Hi. I've been okay, I guess. Nothing really changed since last time. I've been thinking a lot about this thing that happened at a work gathering last week, and it's been bothering me. Maybe we could talk about that.

That sounds like something that really stayed with you. Since nothing else seems urgent right now, let's dive into how that work gathering made you feel and what exactly happened that triggered those strong reactions. Can you walk me through the situation from your perspective?

Well, it was a casual after-work thing at a bar. Everyone was laughing and telling stories, and I just stood there by the table, holding my drink, not really knowing what to say. I tried to jump in a couple times, but my comments fell flat and people just kept talking over me. I ended up leaving early, feeling like I didn't belong there.

It sounds incredibly isolating to be standing there while everyone else is laughing and connected, especially when you feel like your voice isn't being heard. When you left early feeling like you didn't belong, did that thought make things worse, or was it more of a natural reaction to feeling excluded?

It felt like both, honestly. Like, I wasn't surprised that it happened, because I always expect that kind of thing. But at the same time, it just confirmed what I already think about myself—that I'm not interesting enough to be part of those conversations. I guess leaving early was my way of accepting that.

It makes sense that leaving felt like a way to stop the pain, even though it reinforced that belief. When you say you expected that outcome beforehand, does that suggest you were carrying a heavy weight about your own worth going into the room, or did something specific happen during the event that shifted your expectation?

I think I already had that weight before I even walked in. I spent the whole day worrying about what to say, how to act, whether people would think I was boring. So by the time I got there, I was already kind of defeated. The way it actually played out just felt like proof that I was right to worry.

It takes a lot of strength to carry that much anxiety all day long, and it makes complete sense that once you arrived, the world seemed to confirm your fears instantly. That feeling of being "right" about your worries can actually be a very painful trap because it convinces you that the problem lies entirely within you, rather than the situation itself. Could we look at one specific moment where someone laughed at your joke, and then try to find another piece of evidence from that evening that suggested otherwise?

I guess... there was one moment where a coworker actually asked me a question about my weekend plans. I gave a short answer, but she smiled and said it sounded fun. Not really. Most of my life is pretty routine—I go to work, I go home, I watch TV. It's just at the counter where things feel off. When it's slow, I start thinking it's because I'm not good enough at making the sandwiches or wrapping things right, and that's when I feel the worst.

That makes sense; when the rush isn't there, your mind might be filling the silence with worries about your performance. Since you mentioned feeling "not good enough" specifically around the sandwiches and wrapping, could you walk me through a moment when you noticed those doubts popping up while you were working?

Well, just yesterday, there was a stretch where nobody came to the counter for almost an hour. I kept checking the clock, and each minute felt heavier. I started replaying in my head how I might have messed up a customer's order the day before—maybe I put too much mayo or didn't slice the meat thin enough. It's like I just know that's why they're not coming back.

That sounds incredibly exhausting, especially carrying that heavy weight of self-doubt while trying to stay productive. Can you describe exactly what happened in your mind right after that first empty minute passed? Did you notice anyone else looking at the clock or reacting to the silence?

Nobody else seemed to notice, or maybe they just didn't care. The other guy on the grill was busy cleaning his station, not looking at the counter at all. But in my head, I started thinking, "See? They're avoiding you. They know you're not quick enough, not good enough." It's like my brain just jumps straight to that conclusion without any proof.

That interpretation feels very lonely, even though there is zero evidence that anyone is avoiding you or judging your speed. Let's look at the facts from that hour of silence: did anyone actually say anything to you, or did you just fill the gap with your own story about why they weren't there?

No, nobody said anything. There was no complaint, no angry customer, nothing like that. It was just... quiet. And I filled it all up with my own story, like you said. I guess I just assumed the worst because it feels true, even when I know it might not be.

It makes complete sense that your brain jumped to that conclusion because safety usually comes from being needed or seen, so silence feels threatening. However, let's try to separate that feeling from the reality: if you looked around carefully during that hour, did you see anyone else who seemed distracted, tired, or perhaps just taking a break? Or did everyone seem to be doing their normal work as usual?

Now that I think about it, everyone was just doing their normal stuff. The manager was on the phone, the grill guy was prepping for later, and there were a few people at the self-checkout. Nobody looked upset or anything. It was just a normal slow hour. I guess I was the one making it into something bigger than it was.

That shift in perspective is really powerful, and it shows how much your mind can change once we look at the actual scene versus the story we tell ourselves. Since you noticed everyone was doing their normal routine, does that help ease the feeling that you are somehow causing the silence by being "slow"? Or do you still feel a bit alone in that space even though others were fine?

It does help a little, yeah. I mean, logically I can see that it's probably just a slow day or that people are shopping elsewhere. But there's still that little part of me that whispers, "But what if it is you? What if you're the reason they're not coming?" I guess that part doesn't go away that easily, even when I know it might not be true.

That whisper is understandable because our brains often link our worth to our output, but let's try one small experiment to challenge that link. Could you imagine a scenario where someone else made a mistake on a slow day, like forgetting a side dish or dropping a tray, and how would you react to them? Would you assume they are worthless workers, or would you treat them differently?

I'd probably just say "no big deal" and help them clean it up. I'd never think they were a bad worker because of one mistake or a slow hour. So I guess it's not fair to treat myself that way either. It's just harder to be kind to myself than to others, you know?

That is such a compassionate insight, and it highlights the unfairness of holding yourself to a standard you wouldn't apply to anyone else. To make that kindness a habit, could we try a simple mental trick tonight where, instead of waiting for a mistake to happen, you intentionally offer yourself that exact same "no big deal" response when you notice that whisper starting?

Yeah, I think I can try that. Maybe just telling myself "no big deal" when I start to spiral about a slow counter or a messy sandwich. It sounds simple, but I guess it's worth a shot. Thanks for that.

That sounds like a great plan, and I want to encourage you to try it even if it feels awkward at first. For tonight, whenever you catch that spiral about the quiet counter or a messy item, just pause and quietly say "no big deal" to yourself before continuing your task. How does that sound as a starting point for us to try together?

It sounds... doable. I mean, it's just three little words, right? I can give it a try and see what happens. Might feel silly at first, but maybe that's what I need. Thanks for helping me see it that way.

That willingness to try something that feels slightly silly is actually a sign of real courage, because it means you're ready to act despite the discomfort. Since we agreed on the "no big deal" phrase, could you also decide if you'll say it out loud or just whisper it to yourself, and what one specific thing you'll do immediately after saying it to keep moving forward?

I think I'll just whisper it to myself under my breath so nobody else hears. And right after, I'll just keep working—maybe wipe down the counter or restock the napkins. Something small to keep my hands busy and not let my mind wander back into that spiral. That sounds like a good plan.

That is a perfect, practical plan that uses both a gentle reminder and a physical action to ground you. Since we are wrapping up, how does it feel to have a clear, manageable step ready for tonight, and is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we finish?

It feels... lighter, I guess. Like I've got a small tool to use instead of just sitting in that heavy feeling. I think I'm good for now. Thanks for listening and helping me sort this out. I'll try the "no big deal" thing tonight and see how it goes.
