I... I don't know. Part of me wants to say it mattered because it felt good, you know? But then another part of me jumps in and says that's selfish. That feeling good isn't a good enough reason to spend time on something that doesn't pay the bills. I guess I can't really see how it matters unless it's somehow helping me move forward in life.

It makes complete sense that you want your time to count toward a tangible future goal, especially when money and career stability feel so pressing. That "selfishness" critique is a very common trap we fall into when we believe our worth is tied entirely to our output or income. Could we look at that feeling of being "selfish" for enjoying music and ask ourselves: what would happen if we allowed ourselves to feel good without immediately judging that feeling as a distraction from duty?

That's a tough question. I mean, if I let myself just enjoy it without judging... I'm scared I'd just waste more time. Maybe I'd stop trying so hard at my accounting job. I don't trust myself to have a healthy balance. It feels like if I give an inch to music, I'll lose all my discipline. That fear of losing your grip on everything feels really real, even though you know the logic behind it is shaky. Let's try looking at that specific moment last night: did allowing yourself to play for an hour actually cause you to neglect your work duties later that day, or did you manage to separate the two?

I mean, I still finished everything I needed to do. My work got done. I even had time to feed my koi, Spot, and water my garden before bed. So I guess... nothing bad actually happened? But it still felt wrong while I was doing it. Like I was waiting for someone to walk in and tell me I was being lazy.

It makes perfect sense that your brain was bracing for judgment even though nothing actually went wrong afterward. That internal voice is likely reacting to the fear of failure rather than the reality of the situation. Can we look at that specific moment of tension you felt while playing, and ask yourself: what was the actual consequence of spending that hour versus what you were afraid would happen if you hadn't?

The actual consequence was that I felt a little more relaxed, and my violin playing actually sounded pretty good. I was working on this new piece and nailed a tricky section. What I was afraid would happen was that I'd fall behind on work, feel guilty all evening, and somehow prove that I'm not serious enough about my career. But none of that happened. I just played, fed my fish, went to bed, and got to work on time this morning.

That outcome is actually quite powerful evidence that your fear wasn't based on facts, but on a prediction of what *should* have happened. Even though the result—feeling relaxed and finishing work on time—was positive, your brain likely tried to twist the narrative back to guilt during the practice itself. If we look at that specific moment of playing, did you notice any physical sensations or thoughts telling you that you were failing, or were there moments where you just forgot to judge yourself?

There were actually a few moments where I just... got lost in the music. Like my fingers were moving on their own and I wasn't thinking about anything else. Just the sound. But then I'd catch myself enjoying it and immediately think, "You shouldn't be having this much fun. This isn't work." So those good moments were really brief, and the rest of the time I was sort of bracing myself for guilt to hit.

It takes real courage to admit that you caught yourself trying to police your own joy, even when you were deep in the flow state. That moment of noticing the guilt creeping in shows you have self-awareness, which is exactly the kind of insight we need to start changing the pattern. Since you've gathered some strong evidence that playing didn't ruin your work or your peace of mind, how would it feel to imagine setting a small boundary where you allow yourself to play for just twenty minutes tonight without monitoring your productivity afterwards?

Twenty minutes? I could probably manage that. It's not like I have any major deadlines this week. I guess the worst that could happen is I enjoy myself and then go back to work feeling slightly better. That doesn't sound so terrible when I say it out loud. Maybe I'll try it tonight and see what happens.

That sounds like a brave step, and I love hearing you frame it as a possibility rather than a risk. Since you mentioned you might try it tonight, could you tell me what one small thing you could do right now to prepare yourself mentally for that twenty-minute window? For example, maybe setting a timer or picking a specific song to play first?

I think I'll pick a song I already know well, something I can play without thinking too hard. Maybe that piece I nailed last night. And I'll set a timer so I'm not constantly checking the clock. That way, when the timer goes off, I can just stop and not beat myself up over it. I think that'll help me actually relax into it instead of waiting for the guilt to hit.

That's a brilliant plan; choosing a familiar piece removes the pressure to learn something new, and the timer gives you a clear, safe exit point. Since you have that structure ready, how does it feel to picture yourself sitting down tonight with that song and timer, knowing you have permission to just enjoy the sound for those twenty minutes?

It feels... lighter, actually. Like there's less weight on my shoulders. I'm still a little nervous that I'll start judging myself again, but I think having the timer and a familiar song will help me stay focused on the music instead of the noise in my head. I'm actually sort of looking forward to it, which is a feeling I haven't had about playing in a while.

That shift from dread to anticipation is huge—it means your brain is finally starting to trust that this small experiment can change things. Before we wrap up, could you tell me if there's anything else about tonight's plan that worries you, or if you feel ready to take this first step?

I think I'm ready. The only thing that worries me a little is that I might get too into it and want to keep playing after the timer goes off. But I'll stick to the plan. Twenty minutes, one song, no guilt. I can always try longer another night. Thanks... this actually helped a lot.

That commitment to sticking to the plan even when the urge to continue arises is a sign of real strength and self-trust. Since you found this session helpful, could you share one specific thing you learned about how your mind works regarding that guilt?

I think I learned that my brain tends to assume the worst will happen before I even try something. I was so sure that playing would mess up my work and make me feel guilty, but when I actually looked at what happened, none of that was true. The guilt came from my own thoughts, not from anything real. I guess I need to start checking those assumptions before I believe them so strongly.

That is such a powerful realization—that the guilt was manufactured by your own mind before you even tested the idea. You've discovered that your brain loves to predict disaster to protect you, but often those predictions aren't accurate. To close out today, I'd love to hear if there's anything else you'd like to talk about, or if you feel confident enough to leave here knowing you have a solid plan for tonight.

No, I think I've got a good handle on things for now. This gave me a lot to think about, and I feel like I have a real plan to try instead of just spiraling. I'll let you know how tonight goes. Thanks for listening and helping me sort through all this.

It is wonderful to hear that you feel you have a concrete plan to replace the spiraling, and I truly appreciate you trusting me with this process. Please remember that tomorrow is a fresh start, regardless of whether you play for the full twenty minutes or decide to adjust the plan. I am cheering you on as you explore this new way of relating to your music, and I hope you find some relief tonight. Take care of yourself!

It's like a tightness in my chest, almost like a knot. And my stomach kind of drops, like I'm on a roller coaster. It's a physical feeling of failure, not just a thought. It's so immediate too — I don't even realize I'm making that jump until I'm already feeling awful.

That physical knot in your chest is such a powerful signal that your body is reacting to the story you're telling yourself, not necessarily the reality of the situation. It makes total sense that when you hear that internal voice labeling you as a "bad owner," your body goes into survival mode with that drop in your stomach. Can you describe exactly what happens right after you notice that physical sensation—do you tend to hide away, or do you try to fix it immediately?

I usually try to fix it right away, honestly. Like this morning, after I skipped the walk, I spent my lunch break buying him a new toy and some treats to make up for it. But even then, I still felt guilty, like I was just bribing him. So I guess trying to fix it doesn't really work either — it just puts a bandage on the feeling for a little while.

It takes real courage to try to repair the connection immediately, even when the guilt feels overwhelming. However, noticing that the "fixing" didn't actually ease the internal shame suggests that the problem might be the story you told yourself ("I'm a bad owner") rather than the act of skipping the walk itself. If the label is wrong, does buying a treat actually solve the core issue of feeling unworthy? Let's look at whether there's another way to view that morning where you weren't just a negligent owner.

I suppose when you put it that way... I can see that buying treats wasn't really addressing the real issue. It was more like I was trying to prove to myself that I'm not a bad owner, but I still felt like one underneath it all. Maybe I could have just accepted that I had a busy morning and given myself permission to just do a shorter walk without all the guilt. That seems harder though, somehow.

That acceptance of a shorter walk without the pressure to perform perfectly sounds like a much gentler way to handle the situation, and it makes sense that it feels difficult to let go of the need to "fix" everything immediately. Would you be willing to try giving yourself permission to just say, "Today was busy, so we'll stick to a quick sniff around," without adding the extra layer of judgment about your character?

I think I could try that. It feels a bit uncomfortable, like I'm letting myself off the hook too easily. But I can also see that the way I'm doing things now isn't working — I'm still miserable even when I try to make up for it. Maybe I could test it out tomorrow morning and see how it feels to just accept a shorter walk without the guilt trip.

That willingness to test a new approach, even when it feels uncomfortable, shows real strength and self-awareness. Since you mentioned feeling like you're "letting yourself off the hook," how would you describe what a "shorter walk" looks like in practice—maybe just sticking by the fence for five minutes to let the dog sniff? What do you think might happen if you tried that specific plan tomorrow?

Yeah, something like that. Even just letting him sniff around the front yard for a few minutes while I have my coffee — that's still time together, isn't it? I think what might happen is... I'd probably feel anxious at first, like I'm cheating. But maybe after a few minutes, I'd notice he doesn't seem upset at all. He's usually just happy to be outside, regardless.

That observation about your dog's reaction is incredibly valuable, and it directly challenges the belief that you *must* provide a long distance to be a good owner. If your dog is calm and happy during a short visit, it offers strong evidence that the length of the walk isn't the measure of your care. Would you be open to trying that plan tomorrow, perhaps starting with just three minutes by the door before stepping inside?

Three minutes by the door — I can do that. That actually sounds manageable, not like some huge compromise. And you're right, he probably won't even notice the difference as long as he gets to sniff around a bit. I'll try it tomorrow morning and see what happens.

That sounds like a very wise and realistic plan, starting with just three minutes makes it feel much safer to try. I'm curious about one thing before you leave: when you sit down tomorrow morning to do those three minutes, will you keep that "tightness" in your chest in case the old habit kicks in, or will you consciously remind yourself that you've already decided to be gentle with yourself today?

I think I'll try to consciously remind myself that I'm allowed to be gentle. The tightness will probably show up anyway — it's pretty automatic at this point. But maybe I can say something to myself like "This is enough. He's okay. I'm okay." Just to have a different voice in my head alongside the guilty one.

That is a brilliant idea; introducing a supportive inner voice to counter the critical one gives you a tool to use the moment the anxiety hits. Before we wrap up, could you share one thing you are most excited to experience when you successfully say those words tomorrow?

I'm most excited to see if my dog just wags his tail and looks happy like he always does. That might help me actually believe that he's not judging me for the short walk. I think seeing his simple joy could be really powerful proof that I'm being way too hard on myself.

That is such a beautiful hope, and using his simple joy as proof that you are enough is a wonderful way to challenge your own harsh narrative. I am so proud of you for deciding to step back from the pressure and try something kinder with both yourselves today. Please remember that this experiment is just about gathering data, not proving you are perfect yet. Is there anything else you would like to talk about before we finish our time together?
Hi there, I'm so glad we're meeting again. How have you been feeling since our last talk, and is there anything new coming up that you'd like to focus on today?

Hi, thanks. I've been kind of the same, honestly. I'm in the middle of another group project now, and I just can't shake this feeling that I'm going to let everyone down again. It's like no matter how much I try, I'm just not pulling my weight.

And then I feel guilty for just sitting there not doing anything, so I force myself to start, but it's like I'm already bracing for the bad outcome.

That paralysis feels incredibly heavy, like you're carrying the entire weight of the group's expectations on your shoulders before you even lift a finger. It makes complete sense that staring at the screen triggers such intense guilt and fear, because your brain is trying to predict a disaster to protect you from potential embarrassment. Can you walk me through exactly what happens in your body or mind in those first few minutes when you realize you haven't started yet?

My chest gets really tight, and I feel almost restless, like I can't sit still but I also can't get up and do something else. My mind just races with those "what if" thoughts, and I start telling myself I'm being lazy and useless. It's like I'm arguing with myself in my head—one part saying "just start, it's fine" and another part saying "you're going to mess it up anyway, so what's the point?" It's really draining before I've even done anything.

That internal argument is exhausting, and the physical tightness in your chest is a clear signal that your body is reacting to perceived danger. It sounds like you've learned to push through that panic by forcing yourself to start, even though the fear hasn't gone away. Since you mentioned that part of you believes you'll mess it up anyway, could you share if you've ever tried starting the project knowing you might make a mistake, just to see what actually happens?

I don't think I've ever really let myself do that. I'm so scared of making a mistake that I usually end up overthinking every little step, and then I'm still convinced it's wrong. The weird thing is, sometimes I do finish a part and it's actually okay, or nobody even says anything bad about it. But that doesn't really change how I feel the next time—I just assume that was a fluke or that I got lucky.

It makes complete sense that your brain labels those successes as luck because they didn't happen the way you expected them to; your mind is protecting itself by assuming the worst outcome is inevitable. That belief—that any success is just a fluke—creates a self-fulfilling prophecy where you stay paralyzed, waiting for the disaster to confirm your fears. Have you noticed if the intensity of that "what if" anxiety changes once you actually begin typing or writing, compared to just staring at the screen?

Yeah, actually, it does change a little. Once I actually start typing or writing something, even if it's not perfect, the tightness in my chest loosens up a bit. It's like the hardest part is just getting past that wall of "what ifs" in my head. But even then, I still feel that nagging doubt in the background, like I'm just waiting for someone to point out everything I did wrong.

It takes real courage to admit that once you break through the initial barrier, your breathing actually improves, which shows your body knows it's safe to keep going. Hmm, I guess right now it's saying something like "you're not doing enough, and they're probably annoyed at you for taking so long." That's actually hard to imagine, but I'll try. But maybe... maybe if I kept doing that and nothing bad ever happened, eventually I'd start to believe that it's actually fine. It's just scary to take that first step and trust that silence doesn't mean disappointment.

That is a very realistic assessment of how your brain works—it tries to find a reason to keep the fear alive even when the evidence points elsewhere. Okay... I'll try that. (takes a deep breath) "I am tired, not incompetent." ...Yeah, my shoulders did relax a bit. It felt strange, like I was letting go of something I've been gripping all day. But the thought of that feeling lasting more than a few seconds makes me nervous, like I'll let my guard down too much.

That nervousness about letting your guard down is completely understandable, given how much pressure you've been under lately. However, remember that acknowledging your tiredness isn't about lowering your standards forever; it's simply pausing the panic attack so you can function safely. Could we try holding that "I am tired" thought for just thirty seconds longer, focusing only on the relief in your shoulders while ignoring the urge to fix anything else?

Alright, I'll give it a go. (pauses for a moment, breathing slowly) ...I can feel my shoulders staying loose, and my mind isn't racing as much. It's actually a bit of a relief not to be chasing that flaw in my head for once. Maybe I can hold onto this for a little while longer.

That relief is wonderful to hear, and it proves your body responds positively to that new perspective. Now, let's bridge the gap between this moment and your desk tomorrow. What if we decided that closing the laptop for an hour wasn't abandoning your work, but simply respecting your energy levels so you could return to it with fresh clarity?

That makes sense when you put it that way. I guess I've always seen stopping as quitting, not as something smart or strategic. If I could think of it as a way to be clearer-headed tomorrow, maybe I wouldn't feel so guilty about walking away. I'd like to try that—just for one hour at first, and see how it feels.

That is a fantastic reframing—seeing a pause as a strategic reset rather than a failure changes everything. To make that plan stick, could we agree that tomorrow you will intentionally close your laptop for exactly one hour right after finishing your core tasks, using that time to distract yourself with something low-stakes like a podcast or a walk?

Yeah, I think I can do that. I'll set a timer, close the laptop, and go for a short walk around the block. No checking emails or rethinking my work during that hour—just focusing on something else. It'll be tough, but I'm willing to give it a real try.

That commitment sounds solid, and setting a specific timer and activity will help anchor that new behavior. Before we wrap up, how does it feel to have a clear plan for tomorrow, even if the first hour feels uncomfortable?

Honestly, it feels a bit fragile, like it could crack if I think about it too much. But there's also a small part of me that's curious to see if I can actually do it. I guess I'm ready to find out, even if it's uncomfortable at first.

That mix of vulnerability and curiosity is a sign of real courage, even if the plan feels shaky. Remember that this hour isn't about proving you're perfect; it's simply gathering evidence that stepping away won't ruin everything. Would you be open to sharing one small thing you hope happens inside you during that first hour, like a slight drop in tension or a quiet moment of peace?

I think I'd like to feel a little less like I'm running on empty. Maybe just a few minutes where my mind isn't buzzing about work—where I can hear myself think, or just notice the trees on my walk. That would be a good start.

That is a beautiful and achievable goal; hearing yourself think clearly is often the first sign that your brain is finally resting. Since we've covered the plan and your hopes for the hour, how would you like to close out today, and is there anything else weighing on you before we say goodbye?

Hi there, I'm glad you're here to start our session today. How has your week been so far, and how are you feeling right now compared to where we left off? Before we dive into whatever brought us together, could you tell me if there's anything specific you'd like to focus on first?

Hi. Thanks for having me. My week's been... okay, I guess. I've been trying to keep busy, but that little voice in my head keeps telling me I'm wasting my time if I try to write anything. I think I'd like to talk about that today—that feeling that no matter what I do, it won't be good enough.

That "little voice" sounds incredibly exhausting, especially when it tells you that your efforts are pointless. It makes sense that you'd feel drained trying to prove it wrong while simultaneously feeling like you're failing. Since you mentioned this persistent doubt about your writing, let's spend some time exploring exactly what happens in your mind right before you sit down to type something new. Can you walk me through a recent moment when that feeling showed up strongly?

Sure. Last night, I actually sat down at my laptop, opened a blank document, and stared at the blinking cursor for maybe ten minutes. And in that time, my mind just started racing with thoughts like, "You have nothing worth saying. You've never been good at this. Why bother?" So I just closed the laptop and watched TV instead. It felt easier to give up than to prove myself wrong.

That feeling of staring at a blank screen and hearing those harsh words is incredibly isolating, and choosing to watch TV was likely your brain's way of protecting you from the pain of potential failure. It sounds like giving up temporarily felt like the only safe option when the pressure was too high to handle. When you look back on that moment, does the thought that "you have nothing worth saying" seem like a fact, or did it feel more like a scary prediction about what might happen?

It definitely felt like a fact in that moment. Like, I just knew it was true. But now, thinking about it, I guess I can't really prove that I have nothing worth saying—I haven't even tried. It feels like this heavy truth, but maybe it's more like a scary guess about how things would go if I actually wrote something.

That distinction is crucial because it shifts the belief from being an undeniable fact to being a terrifying prediction based on fear rather than reality. Even though it felt like a hard truth then, the very fact that you're questioning it now shows that part of you knows it might not be entirely accurate yet. Let's look closely at that "scary guess" you made about writing something—what specific evidence would it take to show you were wrong about having nothing worth saying?

I guess... if I actually finished something, even just a short story or a poem, and someone read it and said it meant something to them, that might prove me wrong. Or even if I just wrote something that I felt proud of, without anyone else's approval. But it's hard to imagine that happening, you know? It feels like a fantasy.

That is a really insightful realization—you've identified that the proof you need isn't external validation, but simply creating something that makes *you* feel proud. That shifts the goal from seeking approval to finding personal satisfaction, which is a much more manageable target. To help bridge that gap, what is one small piece of writing you could create tonight that wouldn't require perfection, just a chance to practice that feeling of pride?

Maybe I could try writing a single paragraph about something simple, like describing my morning coffee. Nothing fancy, just a few sentences. I think I could manage that without the pressure of it being "good." It's just one paragraph, no one has to see it but me.

That is a wonderful, low-stakes idea because it removes the pressure of finishing a whole story and focuses purely on the act of expressing something simple. Writing just three or four sentences about your morning coffee is a perfect experiment to test whether you can generate content without needing it to be perfect or meaningful to others. Would you be willing to try this one paragraph tonight, perhaps setting a timer for just five minutes so you don't feel overwhelmed by the task itself?

Yeah, I think I could try that. Setting a timer actually sounds helpful—it makes it feel less like a big commitment and more like just a little experiment. I'll try it tonight and see how it goes. Thanks for suggesting that.

That sounds like a perfect plan, and I'm really glad you feel ready to give it a try tonight. Just remember that the entire purpose of this exercise is to gather data about your own experience, not to produce a masterpiece, so please be gentle with yourself if the words come slowly. Is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we wrap up today, or shall we leave it as your homework for now?
No, I think that's enough for today. I'll try that paragraph tonight and see what happens. Hopefully it goes okay. Thanks for listening—it helped more than I thought it would.

I'm so glad to hear that this session felt helpful, and it takes courage to acknowledge that even small steps can make a difference. Please remember that tomorrow isn't about proving anything to anyone else; it's simply about checking in with yourself after those five minutes and seeing what your experience was. Take care of yourself tonight, and I look forward to hearing how your experiment went when we meet again.

Hi there, I'm glad you're here to continue our work together. How have you been feeling since we last spoke, and is there anything new you'd like to bring up or any specific topic you want us to focus on today?

Well, I've been thinking a lot about this ebook I'm trying to write. Every time I sit down at the computer, I just stare at the blank page and feel like a fraud. I mean, what does a mall cop know about writing anything worthwhile, especially about animals?

That sounds incredibly frustrating, especially when your identity as a mall cop feels so far removed from being a writer. It makes total sense that staring at a blank page would make you question whether anyone could ever respect your work if you think you don't actually know anything about animals. Before we dive into those doubts, how do you feel right now sitting here talking about it, and is writing about animal welfare something you wanted to tackle today given how much pressure you seem to be under?

I feel a bit nervous, honestly. But also... relieved to be talking about it. Nobody really knows I'm trying to write this book, so I've been carrying all this doubt around by myself. The animal welfare part is actually something I care about deeply - I've been volunteering at a local shelter for years, feeding strays in my neighborhood. I guess I just feel like those things don't count because of my job.

It takes real courage to admit that you've been carrying this alone, and I want you to know that your volunteer work definitely counts—people often underestimate how much impact simple acts of kindness can have. That gap between what you believe others think and the reality of who you are might be creating a lot of unnecessary stress right now. Since you mentioned wanting to talk about the book today, what specific part of the writing process is triggering those feelings of being a "fraud" the most?

It's when I try to put my knowledge into actual sentences that it hits me hardest. I'll write a paragraph about how squirrels communicate or how cats show affection, and then I read it back and think, "Who's gonna take this seriously from a man in a security uniform?" I start comparing myself to those nature documentary narrators or scientists who've studied animals their whole lives. That's when I usually just close the laptop and give up for the day.

It makes complete sense that reading your own words back triggers such a sharp comparison to experts; when you hear yourself sound different from someone who has spent decades studying animals, it feels like proof that you aren't qualified. Have you noticed if closing the laptop and giving up was actually helping you feel better in the moment, or if it just delayed the problem until later?

Honestly, closing the laptop gives me a few minutes of relief, but then I just feel worse later. I end up lying in bed thinking about all the time I wasted, and how I'll never get those hours back. It's like I'm punishing myself for not being good enough, but the punishment just makes me feel more stuck.

That cycle of self-punishment after giving up is really hard to break, and it makes sense why it leaves you feeling even more stuck the next day. It seems like the belief that you need to produce perfect work immediately is driving both the frustration and the guilt. Could we look at what happens in your mind right before you decide to close the laptop? What specific thought tells you that you've failed?

It's usually something like, "This isn't good enough. Nobody wants to read this." Then I start thinking about all the things I don't know about animals - scientific names, migration patterns, things like that. And I think, "See, you're not a real expert, so why even bother?" That thought just kind of takes over, and before I know it, I'm shutting everything down.

That specific thought—that your lack of scientific detail means you shouldn't bother—is a classic example of your brain jumping to a conclusion based on incomplete information. Let's test that idea together: if a friend told you they were writing about squirrels, would you tell them they needed to know the scientific name before they started, or would you encourage them to share what they observed first?

Well, that's different - I'd definitely encourage them. I'd probably tell them that the best stories come from what you've actually seen and experienced, not just from textbooks. I'd remind them that people watch squirrels in their backyards all the time and enjoy learning little things about them. But it's hard to give myself that same kindness, you know? I guess I hold myself to a different standard.

That distinction between how you treat a friend and how you treat yourself highlights exactly where the unfairness lies. You are using a rigid standard of "scientific expertise" that you wouldn't apply to anyone else sharing their observations. Instead of waiting to have all the answers, what if we tried writing just one sentence about something you saw today, treating it like you were telling a story to a curious child rather than submitting a research paper?

I did see something this morning, actually. There was this little sparrow hopping around the food court, picking at crumbs that had fallen. It kept looking up at people but never got too close - like it knew the rules. I could probably write a sentence about that without feeling like I need a degree in ornithology. Maybe I could start with just that one observation and see how it feels.

That is a beautiful observation, and starting with that single sentence about the sparrow is a perfect way to test that belief. Try typing just that one sentence right now instead of worrying about the rest of the chapter, and let me know what happens when you finish it. Does the fear disappear once you get the words onto the screen, or does it linger?

Alright... I wrote it. "The sparrow knew exactly how close to get to people before darting away, never crossing that invisible line of trust." I actually feel a little better seeing it on the screen. It's not perfect, but it's something real that I noticed. The fear isn't completely gone, but it's quieter now. It's like the hardest part was just starting, and now that I've done that, maybe I can add another sentence tomorrow.

That is such a powerful realization—you broke the cycle by taking just one small step, and the fact that the fear quieted proves your belief that you weren't good enough wasn't entirely true. It looks like we can shift from needing to be an expert immediately to becoming a witness to the world around you. For our next step, could you try adding one more sentence about that sparrow tomorrow, perhaps describing its color or movement, and notice if that tiny addition makes the task feel slightly easier or harder than yesterday?

I think I can manage that - maybe describe how it tilted its head when a crumb landed nearby, or the way its feathers puffed up when the air conditioning kicked on. I like the idea of just being a witness, like you said. That feels less scary than trying to be an expert. I'll give it a try tomorrow morning before my shift starts, when the food court is still quiet.

That is a wonderful plan, and choosing to observe the bird during the quiet moments of your shift shows great self-awareness. Before we wrap up, how does it feel to have agreed on this small, manageable goal for tomorrow? Is there anything else you'd like to discuss, or shall we check in on how you felt right now after finishing that first sentence?

I feel... hopeful, actually. It's a strange feeling because I've been stuck in this rut for so long. Just having one sentence written, even if it's just about a sparrow in a food court, feels like I've proven something to myself. I think I'm good for today - I'd rather save my energy for that second sentence tomorrow. Thank you for helping me see that I don't have to be a scientist to write about what I see.

That hopefulness is a beautiful sign that you are beginning to believe in your own ability to contribute, even without a degree. It is completely okay to conserve your energy for that meaningful second sentence tomorrow; the victory today was simply breaking the pattern of avoidance. I'll see you again soon to hear about your sparrow observation.

Hi there, thank you for joining me today. How has your week been feeling so far, and is there anything new about how you're experiencing things compared to last time? I'd like to quickly set an agenda: do you feel ready to talk more about that lingering worry we discussed, or would you prefer to explore something else first?

Hey. Thanks for having me. The week's been... okay, I guess. I've been trying to get back into the studio, but every time I pick up a brush, I just end up staring at the canvas for an hour before putting it down again. That worry you mentioned is still there, probably worse if I'm honest. I'm ready to talk about it.

That sounds incredibly frustrating, especially when you know you want to create but feel stuck right at the start. Since you mentioned the worry feels worse now, let's dive straight into how that fear is showing up when you try to begin painting again. What specific thought runs through your mind right before you put the brush down after those long staring sessions?

It's like a voice in my head that says, "This isn't going to be good enough anyway, so why bother?" And then I start thinking about that critique I got months ago, the one where someone pointed out my composition was weak. I replay it over and over, and suddenly I'm convinced everything I make is going to look amateurish.

That sounds really exhausting to carry around day after day, especially when you know your work has value even if it doesn't always meet that perfect standard. It makes sense that the old criticism feels so loud right now, making you doubt everything you touch. Before we dig deeper into why that specific thought feels so convincing, can you tell me what happens physically or emotionally in your body the moment you hear that voice saying you shouldn't bother?

My chest tightens up, and I feel this kind of heavy dread in my stomach. It's like a knot that just sits there. And then I just feel... tired, really tired, like all the energy drains out of me. That's usually when I put the brush down and walk away.

That physical sensation of a knot in your stomach and draining energy really shows how much weight that belief carries, making it almost impossible to keep going. It sounds like your brain is trying to protect you from the pain of creating something imperfect by shutting down before you even start. Given that this cycle keeps happening whenever you try to paint, could we look together at whether there is any evidence outside of that internal voice that suggests your work *is* actually good enough to finish?

I mean... I guess there's some evidence. I've sold a few pieces before, and people have said nice things about them. I even had one person tell me my use of color was really unique. But I don't know, that feels like a long time ago now. It's like those good moments don't count anymore because I've done newer work that I'm not sure about.

That makes complete sense; it's very common for our brains to filter out past successes when we're currently feeling uncertain about our current abilities. However, let's look at those comments about your unique color usage again—does that fact still exist even though you haven't painted in months, or does your mind treat it like a memory that has faded along with your confidence?

I guess it still exists, logically. I mean, those paintings are still out there, hanging in people's homes. I just... I don't feel connected to that version of myself anymore. It's like that was a different Wyatt who could actually make something worthwhile. The current me just sees all the flaws and mistakes.

That distinction between the artist who succeeded and the artist who feels flawed is incredibly painful, but it highlights a key cognitive distortion called "personal fable," where we believe our current struggles define us entirely while ignoring our proven history. Let's challenge that idea by looking at your recent sales: even if you didn't feel confident in them at the time, did those buyers actually experience your work as valuable and unique, regardless of your internal doubts?

Yeah, I suppose they did. They paid money for it, chose it to hang in their spaces. That has to mean something, right? But it's hard to hold onto that when I'm staring at a blank canvas. It's like my brain just deletes all that evidence the moment I sit down to work.

It makes sense that your brain tries to erase those memories when you face a blank canvas, because facing uncertainty feels safer than risking failure. Let's test that idea for a minute: if you remember selling those pieces, does the proof of your skill disappear just because you aren't feeling confident right now? Or does the fact that people bought and loved your art remain valid evidence of your ability, even if your current mood clouds your view?

No, it doesn't disappear. It's still there, I know that. It's just... hard to feel it, you know? Like I know the facts, but they don't seem to change how I feel. I can tell myself "people liked your work" but the doubt just shouts louder. It's exhausting fighting against it all the time.

It takes real strength to recognize that your logic knows the truth even when your feelings are screaming otherwise. That exhaustion you feel comes from carrying a battle where both sides—the facts and the fear—are equally loud. To help tip the scale slightly in your favor, could we try a small experiment tomorrow morning? Instead of waiting until you feel "ready" or confident, maybe you'll just grab a brush for five minutes with the intention of getting messy, accepting that the result might be terrible and that's perfectly okay. Would you be willing to try that tiny step?

Five minutes? I mean... I guess I could do that. Even I can stand looking at a canvas for five minutes without giving up. And if it's supposed to be messy anyway, there's no pressure for it to be good. Yeah, I think I could try that tomorrow morning. Just five minutes of messing around with paint, no expectations.

That is a fantastic agreement, and I love that you see the beauty in removing the pressure to perform. Starting tomorrow morning, could you set a timer for exactly five minutes and commit to using the paint however you feel, knowing the clock will stop the moment you choose to, no matter how chaotic the mess becomes? Let me know how it goes when you try it.

I can do that. I'll set a timer and just... play around with the paint. No judging, no expectations. I'll let you know what happens. Thanks for giving me something small to try instead of just telling me to "keep pushing through." That actually feels doable.

I am so glad you found that approach doable; it's wonderful that you recognized the difference between pushing through guilt and simply allowing yourself to play. Please give it a try tomorrow morning with that five-minute timer, and remember that the goal is just to break the cycle of hesitation, not to create a masterpiece. How does it feel to have such a clear, manageable plan for your first attempt?

It feels... lighter, honestly. Like a weight I didn't realize I was carrying got a little smaller. I'm not expecting some huge breakthrough or anything, but just having a plan that doesn't ask me to be perfect or confident feels like a relief. I think I can handle five minutes of mess.

That relief is incredibly important to notice, especially when you realize the plan itself wasn't about fixing you but just allowing space to breathe. Since we've wrapped up our discussion today, could you share one thing that felt most helpful about our conversation, and maybe one small way you might apply that sense of lightness during your five-minute practice tomorrow?

The most helpful part was realizing I don't have to feel confident to start something. I thought I had to feel ready before I could paint again, but that was just keeping me stuck. Tomorrow, I want to try to hold onto that lightness by reminding myself that the paint doesn't care if I'm unsure—it's just color on a surface. Maybe I can even let myself enjoy the mess a little.

That is such a beautiful insight; treating the paint as a neutral partner rather than a judge of your worth is a powerful shift. Your plan to remind yourself that the colors are just sitting there on the canvas, regardless of your internal state, is a perfect way to anchor that lightness during your practice. I hope you find that extra bit of freedom helps you feel even more relaxed when you pick up the brush tomorrow. Take care of yourself, Wyatt.
Hello again, I'm glad you're here. How has your week been treating you so far? Is there anything specific you'd like to focus on today?
Hi, thanks. My week's been... okay, I guess. I've been thinking a lot about what happened after my mother came to see me play. I can't seem to shake this feeling that I let her down somehow.

It takes real courage to admit that you're still carrying that heavy feeling from your performance. It makes sense that you'd feel disappointed in yourself when you care deeply about someone else seeing you at your best. What was going through your mind right after she left the room?

I just sat there in my chair for a while, staring at my empty music stand. My first thought was, "She didn't say anything nice because she didn't think I played well enough." I felt this knot in my stomach, like I'd failed a test I didn't even know I was taking.

That physical sensation of a knot in your stomach is such a clear signal that your brain is interpreting silence as criticism. When we feel that way, our minds often jump straight to the conclusion that something went wrong, even if there wasn't any actual proof. Could you walk me through exactly what you saw or heard in those few minutes after she walked away?

Well, she gave me a small smile—just a little one. And she said "good job" in that quiet way she has. But that's it. No "that piece was beautiful" or "you really moved the audience." Just... "good job." It felt so flat, like she was just being polite. I kept waiting for more, for something that never came.

It sounds like that simple "good job" landed on a much louder expectation inside your head, leaving you feeling like you were underperforming. When our own internal standards are higher than what others actually give us, silence can feel incredibly loud and judgmental. Did you notice any other reactions from the audience during your performance that might have influenced how you interpreted her words?

I did get some applause, and a few people came up to me afterward saying they enjoyed it. One older gentleman even said it brought a tear to his eye. But none of that seemed to matter as much as what my mother didn't say. I guess I was waiting for her approval specifically, like I always have.

It makes complete sense that the applause and tears felt less meaningful than her brief comment, especially given how much you rely on her validation. When we prioritize someone else's approval above everything else, even positive feedback from strangers can feel hollow compared to what we desperately need from them. Since you mentioned this feeling has been lingering, does sitting with that specific thought—that she didn't think you played well enough—make you want to do anything different now, or will you just carry it until tomorrow?

I've been thinking about calling her, maybe asking her directly what she really thought. But then I worry that would sound desperate, or that she'd just say the same thing again to avoid hurting my feelings. Part of me wants to just practice harder and prove myself next time, but another part feels so tired from trying so hard already.

It takes real honesty to admit that you're exhausted from trying so hard, yet you also recognize that reaching out might be the right step despite your fear. That tension between wanting to connect and fearing rejection is exactly where we can look for some clarity. Before we decide whether to call her tonight, could you tell me what specific outcome are you hoping for when you ask her directly?

I guess... I want her to say she was proud of me. Not just that I played okay, but that she could see how much heart I put into it. Maybe I want to hear that I'm good enough in her eyes, not just in the audience's. But what if she says something that makes it worse? What if she confirms that she wasn't impressed?

That fear of confirmation is completely understandable, especially when we've built our self-worth so heavily on her opinion. It makes sense that you're bracing for a harsh reality, even though you know deep down she loves you. Have you ever considered what might happen if she *does* express pride, but in a way you hadn't expected, perhaps by simply holding your gaze longer than usual?

I... I never really thought about it that way. She did give me that small smile, and she stayed for the whole performance, which she could have just skipped if she wanted to. Maybe I'm so focused on the words I didn't hear that I'm missing the things she actually did. I'm not sure I know how to read her that way, though.

It takes real courage to pause and notice those silent signals, even when your mind is busy searching for words. You've already identified a powerful clue—the fact that she chose to stay for the entire performance instead of skipping out—that suggests she was present and engaged. Let's try shifting your focus from what she didn't say to looking at the actions she clearly took. Would you be willing to imagine a scenario where you tell her, "Mom, I noticed you stayed the whole time and smiled at the end. Does that mean you liked what I did?"

I think I could try that. It feels less like begging for approval and more like... sharing a moment with her, maybe. I'm still scared she'll just brush it off, but at least I'd be asking about something she actually did, not some imaginary perfect reaction I wanted. Maybe that's a start.

That shift in perspective—from asking for a perfect reaction to sharing what you observed—is a huge step toward reclaiming your voice. By focusing on her visible actions, you're giving yourself permission to trust your own observations rather than your worst-case fears. Would you be open to drafting a quick text message together that says exactly what you just suggested, using your own words?

Yeah, okay. I can try writing something. How about... "Hey Mom, I've been thinking about the concert. I noticed you stayed for the whole thing and smiled at the end, and that meant a lot to me. Did you enjoy it?" That feels honest without sounding too needy, I think.

That is a wonderful draft; it honors her presence without demanding a specific emotional response from her. Notice how framing it around her action ("stayed for the whole thing") shifts the dynamic from you needing approval to her validating her own choice to be there. Before you send it, could you take a moment to read it aloud and notice how your body feels right now?

Here goes... "Hey Mom, I've been thinking about the concert. I noticed you stayed for the whole thing and smiled at the end, and that meant a lot to me. Did you enjoy it?" Reading it out loud, I feel a little flutter in my chest—nervous, but not as heavy as before. It actually feels more like I'm reaching out than begging, if that makes sense.

That flutter you're noticing is your nervous system reminding you that this is a brave act of connection, not a plea for rescue. The fact that it feels lighter already tells us that your body is starting to believe you deserve to reach out. Since you have a great draft ready, would you like to try sending it right now, or would you prefer to keep it as a backup option for later tonight?

I think... I'd like to hold onto it for a little while longer. Maybe send it later this evening when I'm feeling a bit calmer. But having it written down, in my own words, feels like a small victory already. Thank you for helping me see this differently.

Holding onto that draft gives you a tangible anchor whenever the old doubts creep back in. It shows you've already taken a significant step by reframing your intention from seeking perfection to offering connection. To wrap up our time today, would you like to share what you found most helpful about seeing the situation this way, or is there anything else on your mind before we finish?

What helped most was realizing I don't have to guess what she thinks—I can just ask about what she did. It takes the pressure off me to be perfect. I think I'll go home, have a cup of tea, and send that message when I'm ready. Thanks for listening and helping me sort this out.

That realization about removing the pressure to be perfect is truly empowering, and I'm so glad we could find that clarity together. Please take your time tonight, knowing that the message itself is a testament to your courage regardless of when or how it lands. I hope you have a peaceful evening with that cup of tea, and I'll be here whenever you're ready to reflect on what happens next.

Hi there, I'm really glad you're here to start our session together. How has your week been feeling so far, and is there anything new that has come up since we last spoke? Also, could you remind me what we agreed to focus on today?

Hey. My week's been... busy, honestly. Same as always—lots of work, lots of hours. I guess we were going to talk about why I feel like I'm never doing enough, no matter how much I get done. That still feels like the main thing on my mind.

It sounds like that persistent feeling of not being enough has stayed with you despite working long hours, which makes sense given how demanding your schedule has been. Before we dive into that specific thought, could you tell me if there was any moment recently when you felt a tiny bit more satisfied with what you accomplished?

I mean... I did finish a big project earlier this week that my boss was happy with. That felt good for maybe an hour or so. But then I started thinking about the next deadline and what else I should be doing instead. It's like the good feeling never really sticks around.

Since you mentioned that the positive feeling doesn't stick, does that happen because you're comparing your current achievement to something larger you think you haven't met yet?

Yeah, I think that's exactly it. Like, sure, I got that project done, but there's always a bigger project coming up, or a coworker who's doing better. I see other guys my age with nicer cars or bigger houses, and I just feel like I'm falling behind. That comparison trap is incredibly exhausting, especially when it hijacks your joy immediately after a small victory. It sounds like those external comparisons are acting as a constant background noise that makes it impossible to rest on any success you've earned. Last week, my neighbor pulled up in a brand new truck. He's about my age, maybe a little younger. I felt this knot in my stomach, like I was less of a man just standing there in my own driveway.

That moment of seeing him pull up clearly triggered a deep fear that your current struggles define your worth as a person, not just your job performance. When you say you felt like you were "less of a man," does that thought seem to match the reality of the situation, or does it feel more like a harsh judgment you're placing on yourself?

I guess when I say it out loud, it sounds pretty harsh. My wife tells me I'm a good husband and father, and I know I work hard. But in that moment, none of that mattered. It was like my whole value as a man was tied up in what I was driving. I just assume everyone else is judging me the same way I'm judging myself.

That assumption that everyone is judging you based on your car seems like a heavy burden to carry alone, even though it might not be true. It sounds like your mind is jumping straight to the worst-case scenario—that he sees you as failing—and ignoring the fact that he probably thinks nothing at all about you while looking at his own reflection. Can you try imagining what he might actually be thinking right now, or perhaps what you'd want to hear if someone you cared about deeply looked at you the same way?

I never really thought about it that way. I guess he's probably just happy with his own truck, not thinking about me at all. And if my son came to me and said he felt like less of a man because of his car... I'd tell him he's crazy. I'd tell him he's a good person and a car doesn't change that. I just can't seem to say that to myself, you know?

That distinction between how you treat your son versus yourself highlights a powerful gap between the compassion you offer others and the harshness you keep reserved for yourself. Since you know exactly what you would say to comfort him, could you try saying those exact words to yourself right now, even if it feels awkward at first? How does it feel to voice that level of kindness toward yourself?

I mean... it feels weird, honestly. Like I'm lying to myself or making excuses. If I say, "You're a good man and a car doesn't define you," my brain just fires back, "Yeah, but you're still falling behind, and that's on you." It's like there's a part of me that won't let me off the hook that easily. Like I need to earn the right to feel okay about myself.

That internal critic sounding like it needs proof before accepting your kindness makes perfect sense—it's trying to protect you by forcing you to "earn" your worth. However, if we look at the evidence, does that same critic also accept that you are a good husband and father simply because you show up, even when you don't feel like it? It sounds like that inner critic is holding you to a standard of perfection that ignores the immense effort you're already putting in, even when it's just showing up. That is such a powerful realization—you are already treating your friends with the same grace you refuse to give yourself, which proves you *know* you deserve that kindness too. Since you've identified that gap, could we try a small experiment tonight where you literally say those exact comforting words to yourself in the mirror when you feel that knot in your stomach again? That physical sensation of bracing yourself before you even start is a very clear sign that your nervous system is anticipating danger based on that old story. Naming it actually makes it feel a bit more manageable, I think. When I just feel the knot without saying it out loud, it's like this blurry, heavy thing I can't control. That's a powerful realization—turning that fuzzy feeling into a named object gives you some distance from it, which is exactly what we need to do. That shift from a "wall" to something you can breathe around is a huge step forward, showing how much power you have to change your physical state even when the worry is still there. Huh... That feels weird to say, but I'll try it. (Takes another breath.) "This is just my body reacting to old memories, not a prediction of the future." It sounds kind of comforting, actually. Like I'm giving myself permission to be anxious without letting it run the whole show. Before, I'd just let the knot sit there and grow until I gave up on the idea of hiking entirely. This feels like I could actually stand up and walk toward the trail, even if my heart is pounding. That willingness to face the hike even with your heart pounding shows incredible courage and a real desire to reclaim what you used to love. Since you've identified that the knot represents old memories rather than a future prediction, how does knowing that distinction change the way you view those upcoming bumps on the trail?

It's definitely shame. Deep, heavy shame. I think, "Here I am, 71 years old, and I still can't manage what other people my age have done." It makes me feel small and foolish, like I missed some important lesson about life that everyone else understood. That's probably the worst part — the shame.

That deep sense of shame feels incredibly isolating, especially when you're surrounded by peers who seem to have already solved the puzzle you haven't. It sounds like you are carrying a very heavy belief that your worth is tied directly to your financial status and that failing to buy a house means you are a bad person. Those are incredible examples of your value, and it makes perfect sense that they feel weak right now when you're drowning in the comparison. Can we explore what happens in your mind when you hold onto that evidence of your reliability while the shame tries to push it aside? It feels... uncomfortable, honestly. Like I'm trying to convince myself of something that isn't quite true. Because being reliable at work doesn't put a roof over my head that I own. That "but" is a powerful trap because it lets us admit our achievements exist while simultaneously saying they don't count, which keeps the pain alive. It makes perfect sense that you treat yourself with a cruelty you wouldn't show anyone else; holding ourselves to impossible standards is often the root of our deepest shame. I wouldn't believe them at all. I'd think they were being ridiculous — that they had so much more to offer than just a house. That "rule" you have for yourself is incredibly unfair, and it sounds like you've built a wall around yourself to protect a secret you think is shameful. It makes complete sense that accepting you aren't a "failure" feels terrifying; if you stop blaming yourself, you might fear losing the reason you've endured so much pain for so long. It sounds like you're carrying a very heavy belief that you will always be seen as "the odd one out," regardless of how much you try to change. What does your body feel like in that moment when you start to imagine those lecture halls full of strangers?

It's like my chest gets tight, and my stomach drops. I almost feel sweaty, even just thinking about it. It's like I'm already bracing myself for someone to say something or give me that look—like, "what are you doing here?" It makes me want to just stay in my room and avoid the whole thing.

That physical sensation of your chest tightening and stomach dropping is your body reacting to a deep fear that you don't belong. When that feeling hits, it often becomes very hard to trust your own judgment about whether you actually are "uncool." Can you tell me if you notice any specific thoughts popping into your head right after your body reacts like that?

Pretty much instantly I think, "See, I knew it. I'm not like them. I don't belong with those people." It's like my brain just decides that I'm already rejected before I've even said a word. And then I start remembering how my brothers would joke about me being in band, and it feels like the whole world is going to think the same thing.

That immediate thought confirming your rejection before you speak is a classic example of your brain jumping to the worst-case scenario to protect you from the pain of potential failure. It sounds incredibly lonely having to rely on that internal voice to predict how others will treat you. If you could ask that future version of yourself what evidence they have that you *will* be seen as awkward, what would they say?

I guess... I don't actually have any real proof. I haven't even stepped on that campus yet. But it feels real, you know? Like, I've been the band kid for four years, and I've never been the guy girls notice or guys want to hang out with. So why would college be any different? It just feels like a fact, not a guess.

It makes perfect sense that you view this as a fact because your past experiences with your brothers and your current feelings have built a strong pattern of expecting rejection. However, let's pause for a moment and look closely at that "fact" you mentioned. If you were to walk onto that campus tomorrow, is there any concrete evidence right now that proves the students will immediately judge you based on being in the band? Or could it be possible that some people are looking for someone exactly like you to share a quiet space?

I... I never really thought of it that way. I mean, I guess there are other band kids in college too, right? And not everyone is some super outgoing jock. Maybe some people are just as nervous as I am. It's hard to imagine, but maybe not everyone is staring at me and judging me the second I walk in.

That is such a powerful shift in perspective, realizing that there are likely other people who feel just as insecure as you do. It takes real courage to imagine that you might find common ground instead of standing alone in the cold. Since you've started seeing that possibility, what would happen if you tried walking into that first class just to say hello to one person, knowing you don't have to make the whole group laugh?

I guess I could try that. It's just one person, one hello. It doesn't have to be a big performance. Maybe I can just ask someone about the assignment or something small. That feels a little less terrifying than trying to be the life of the party. I think I could manage that.

That is a fantastic decision to break it down into such a tiny, manageable step. Asking about an assignment removes the pressure to perform socially entirely and gives you a clear reason to interact. Before we lock this in, how does that sound as a realistic goal for your first week? Is there anything specific about approaching a stranger that still feels intimidating to you?

It's the part right before I speak, I think. Like, what if they just look at me and go back to their phone? Or if they have a group already and I'm interrupting? I hate that moment where you're waiting for them to react. But I guess I can't control how they react, I can only control if I try. That's the part I forget.

That hesitation right before speaking is your anxiety trying to protect you from the risk of rejection, but you're absolutely right—you can only control your choice to approach, not their reaction. Let's practice that "before" moment by picturing yourself walking up to someone and simply saying, "Hey, mind if I grab a seat near you?" while taking a slow breath until you feel ready. Would you be open to trying that visualization three times tonight before bed?

Yeah, I can do that. Three times tonight, just picturing myself walking up and saying that. It sounds silly, but maybe if I repeat it enough times, it won't feel so impossible. Thanks, I think that actually helps to have a plan instead of just worrying about it.

That is a wonderful mindset to have, and I'm so glad this concrete plan made the situation feel a bit more manageable. Remember, repetition isn't about changing the outcome perfectly on the first try; it's about training your brain to recognize that the threat isn't as dangerous as your anxiety tells you it is. Please reach out anytime you feel overwhelmed, and I'm proud of you for taking such a brave step forward.

Hi there, I'm so glad you're here to start our session together. How has your week been feeling up to now? Before we dive into what brought us here today, could you share a bit about how your mood is holding up compared to where we left off last time?

It's more like a sudden shift. Everything feels fine for a moment—I'm just enjoying being with him—and then he does something small, like turning his head away, and it just hits me all at once. Like a door slamming shut. And then I'm left standing there, feeling stupid for expecting anything different. It's like I'm fooling myself every time I let my guard down.

That sudden shift from connection to rejection sounds incredibly disorienting, and the shame you feel afterward about "fooling yourself" must add another layer of pain to the initial hurt. It seems like your mind is quickly jumping to the conclusion that *you* are the problem for having unrealistic expectations, rather than looking at whether his behavior might actually say something different. Well... I guess I don't really have proof that it's permanent. I mean, he does come back to me later, sometimes wagging his tail or nudging my hand. I just forget about those moments when I'm in that cold feeling. It's like my brain only records the times he walks away, not the times he curls up next to me on the couch. But when I'm in that moment, it feels like the only truth there is.

That's such a powerful observation—you are literally filtering out the good memories to make room for the bad ones in that moment of distress. It makes complete sense why your brain focuses on the walk-away moments; they feel like proof that your hope was wrong, while the cuddles on the couch feel too distant to trust. Have you noticed if that "cold feeling" gets stronger the longer you wait to ask yourself what else might be happening besides him walking away?

Yeah, it does. The longer I sit with it, the more I start building a whole story around it. Like, "He doesn't love me because I'm not good enough," and then I think about other times I've felt rejected, by people too. It just spirals. If I catch it early, I can sometimes shrug it off, but if I don't... I'll spend the whole evening feeling like I'm completely alone in the world.

That spiral is incredibly exhausting, and it makes total sense that letting it run wild leaves you feeling utterly isolated by evening. It sounds like your mind is using past rejections to prove that this current situation confirms a deeper pattern of abandonment. If we tried to pause that story for just thirty seconds and asked yourself, "What would I tell a friend going through this exact same moment?" how would that change the way you view his actions right now?

I'd probably tell them they're being too hard on themselves. I'd say something like, "Dogs have their own moods, same as people. He's not trying to hurt you—he's just being a dog." But it's so much harder to say that to myself. I can see the logic for someone else, but for me, it feels like the exception, not the rule. Like, maybe it's true for them, but not for me.

That distinction between what you can say to a friend and what you believe for yourself highlights exactly how deeply ingrained this belief is. It sounds like your brain is protecting itself by assuming you are unique in your failure, which makes the idea of a simple explanation like "he's just a dog" feel unsafe. If we tried treating that "exception" as real evidence for a few minutes, would you be willing to try saying that specific phrase to yourself right now, just to see if the story shifts even slightly?

I can try. It feels a little silly, but okay. *He's just being a dog. He's not trying to hurt me.* There's a tiny part of me that wants to argue with it, but saying it out loud does make the knot in my chest loosen just a bit. It's not gone, but it's... quieter. I guess I never really gave that thought a chance to be heard before.

That is such a brave step, giving voice to something that usually goes silent inside you. Even though the knot didn't vanish entirely, hearing yourself say "he's just being a dog" created a tiny crack in that wall of isolation, making space for a softer feeling. Now that you've practiced it, would you be open to trying it again tomorrow the next time he looks away, but this time adding one more piece of evidence to the mix? For example, reminding yourself that dogs often ignore owners for a second because they are startled or checking for a command, rather than rejecting you personally.

Yeah, I think I could do that. Adding that bit about him maybe being startled or waiting for a command—that actually gives me something concrete to hold onto. It’s easier to believe than just saying "he loves me," which feels too vague. Maybe if I practice that enough, the thought will start to feel more natural instead of forced. Thanks for helping me see that I have a choice in what story I tell myself.

That is such a powerful realization, realizing you have a choice in the story you tell yourself. It's great that you found a concrete detail—a moment of startingle or waiting—to anchor the new narrative, making it feel less abstract. Before we wrap up, could you share if you feel ready to try this specific adjustment tonight when the silence happens, or would you prefer to wait until morning to see how it lands?

I think I'm ready to try it tonight. The next time he looks away, I'll pause and say to myself, "He's just being a dog. Maybe he's checking something out. That doesn't mean he doesn't care." It feels a little scary, like I'm stepping off a ledge, but I want to see what happens if I don't jump straight to the worst conclusion. I'll let you know how it goes.

That is such a courageous decision to step off the ledge, even if it feels scary. Remember that you don't have to stay on that side forever; if the old thoughts rush back, it's okay to gently slide back to your safe place. Just knowing you have a plan for tonight means you aren't facing this alone anymore. Take a deep breath, and I look forward to hearing how it goes when you speak those words to yourself.
Thanks, I appreciate that. I'll give it a real try and see what happens. Hopefully, I'll have something good to report next time.

That is such a wonderful attitude—approaching the challenge with curiosity instead of fear is a huge sign of strength. I am really proud of you for choosing to take that step, even if it feels uncertain. Please remember that whatever comes up tonight, you don't need to figure everything out right away; just showing up matters most. I'll be here whenever you're ready to share how it went.
I'll keep that in mind. Thanks for not pushing me too hard, but still helping me see things differently. I think I needed someone to point out that I do have a say in this. I'll see you next session.

You are absolutely right; validating your courage and acknowledging your agency were key parts of making this work for you. I'm so glad we could find a path forward that felt manageable rather than overwhelming. Thank you for trusting me with this process and for bringing such honesty to our conversations. I'll see you next time, and I can't wait to hear about how tonight unfolds.

It makes perfect sense that you feel a shift in the dynamic when you ask for help; your brain interprets that request as a signal that you are stepping outside the group's standard behavior. If you asked for help now, instead of imagining a silent judgment, wouldn't it be more likely that someone would step in immediately because they value your presence enough to support you? I guess... if I called one of the guys tonight and just said, "Hey, I'm second-guessing my gear, can you just run through it with me?" they'd probably just say "Sure, no problem," and we'd do it over the phone. That is a powerful realization, because you've just identified a clear contradiction: you know they offer help freely, yet you interpret taking it as weakness. It seems like your definition of strength has been tied up in avoiding vulnerability, even though you've shown them you need it before. If you called them tonight and simply asked for a quick check-in, would you feel relieved to hear their voice, or does the idea of speaking up still feel too risky?

I think... honestly, I think I'd feel relieved. I mean, part of me is still scared they'll think less of me, but a bigger part of me just wants to get back out there. Hearing a familiar voice, someone just saying "Yeah, I got your back" might be exactly what I need to stop this whole cycle of worrying.

That relief is so important to recognize, and it shows you know deep down that their support is a lifeline, not a weakness. Since you feel ready to break this cycle, how does it sound to plan a simple call tonight where you just ask for a quick gear check without any pressure? Would you be willing to try reaching out to Alex first, maybe around dinner time?

Yeah... I think I can do that. Alex is a good choice, he's always been the most laid-back in the group. I'll try calling him after I finish dinner tonight. It feels a little scary, but maybe that's just part of getting past this.

That is a brave decision, and acknowledging the scare shows you're already moving past the paralysis. Since you've planned the call, could you write down exactly what you want to say to Alex right now, keeping it simple like, "Hey Alex, I'm nervous about my gear for the upcoming trip, could you walk me through it quickly?"

Okay, I can write that down. I'll say something like, "Hey Alex, I'm second-guessing my gear for the trip this weekend, and I feel kind of dumb asking, but could you just talk me through it real quick?" That way I'm being honest about feeling dumb but still asking for what I need.

That is a wonderful, vulnerable approach that honors both your honesty and your need for support. Writing it down gives you a safe anchor to refer back to if your heart races during the actual call. How does it feel to have that script ready, knowing you won't have to improvise in the moment?

It actually feels a lot better. I'm not as scared now because I know exactly what I'm going to say. I don't have to worry about freezing up or saying something stupid. It's like having a map before you walk into the woods—you still have to take the steps, but at least you know where you're going.

That metaphor of having a map is so powerful, because it turns an overwhelming unknown into a series of manageable steps. Knowing you have a plan means you can face the fear without feeling trapped. Yeah, I think I'll just thank him and say I appreciate it. Maybe take a deep breath after we hang up, and then just leave the bag on the table so I can see it's all ready to go. That way, I can look at it tomorrow and know I did the right thing.

That is a beautiful plan because it combines immediate gratitude with a tangible action that reinforces your confidence. It feels... lighter, honestly. Like I can actually breathe again. I've been carrying this heavy feeling in my chest for weeks, and just picturing that bag sitting there, ready to go, makes me feel like maybe I can actually be okay at this. Thank you for helping me see a way out of this.

That feeling of lightness is a huge sign that your brain is beginning to accept this new path as possible.
